the relationship between distance and torque seems like magic to me. what is actually happening to increase torque with a longer lever?
Answer:
Think of torque as “twist power.” A lever turns around a pivot, and your push tries to sweep the lever in a circle. The farther your hand is from the pivot, the bigger the circle your hand traces. Pushing at the edge of a door is easier than pushing near the hinges because your force is applied farther out, giving it more “twisting reach.” In simple terms: the turning effect equals your push multiplied by how far from the pivot you apply it. Double the distance, double the twist. That’s why wrenches have long handles and why door handles aren’t next to the hinges.

What’s actually happening under the hood is a trade: distance for force. When the lever rotates a small angle, a hand that’s farther out travels a longer arc. If you keep pushing with the same force over that longer path, you do more work for the same angle of rotation. That extra work shows up as a larger twist on the pivoted object. So a long lever doesn’t create energy from nowhere—it lets you move your hand farther so the lever can push harder where it matters. Picture a merry-go-round: a gentle shove at the rim spins it up; the same shove near the center barely does anything, because your push has almost no “reach” to twist it.

Question: what does the peer reviewed material say about mosquito repellent? what works? what doesn't?
Answer:
Decades of lab tests, field trials, and systematic reviews converge on a simple picture: the repellents that reliably work are a small, well-studied group that “scramble” the mosquito’s nose. Top performers are DEET, picaridin, IR3535, and oil of lemon eucalyptus’s refined ingredient PMD (para-menthane-3,8-diol). In peer‑reviewed head‑to‑head studies, 20–30% DEET or picaridin and about 20% IR3535 typically give several hours of protection; 30–40% PMD works too, though often for a bit less time and can vary by species. Clothing treated with permethrin doesn’t go on skin but is strongly supported by trials for reducing bites (and ticks). “Spatial” repellents like metofluthrin mats/coils can create a small protective bubble in still air, and simple fans help by blowing away your carbon‑dioxide “scent trail,” both reducing landings in controlled studies. Think of these as layers of an invisible fence: skin repellent, treated fabric, and a light breeze.

What doesn’t hold up well under scrutiny are most gadgets and many plant-based shortcuts. Citronella, peppermint, or lavender oils can repel briefly in the lab, but protection outdoors often fades within 30–60 minutes; citronella candles in particular show little real-world benefit. Wristbands and clip-ons only protect the postage-stamp of skin right next to them; the rest of you is still a buffet. Ultrasonic devices, smartphone apps, vitamin B or garlic supplements, and bug zappers have repeatedly failed to prevent bites in controlled studies (zappers mainly kill harmless insects). In short: pleasant smells and clever electronics rarely beat a mosquito’s biology.

Practical takeaways from the evidence: pick an EPA-registered repellent and match strength to need (everyday yard work: ~20% DEET or picaridin; high-risk travel: similar or a bit higher, reapplying as directed). Apply sunscreen first, repellent second; avoid combo products. DEET and picaridin are considered safe when used as directed, including in pregnancy; PMD products are not recommended for children under 3 years. Use permethrin on clothing and gear only, never directly on skin. Boost protection with long sleeves, intact screens, removing standing water, and a fan on the patio. Picture it like home security: lock the doors (skin repellent), fence the yard (treated clothing), and turn on the porch light and breeze—each layer makes you a less inviting target.

Question: when dogs of different colors breed their descendants can have patches of either color instead of a mixture. why does that not happen on humans?
Answer:
Think of color in skin and hair as coming from millions of tiny “pigment factories” spread across the body. In most humans, those factories are everywhere and they all follow roughly the same set of instructions. When parents with different skin tones have a child, the child inherits many small instruction changes from each parent. Most of these changes simply nudge the factories to make a bit more or a bit less pigment. Add them up across the whole body and you get a smooth, in‑between tone—like mixing two cans of paint and rolling one even coat over the wall.

Many dogs, by contrast, carry special “pattern” switches. Before birth, pigment cells spread out across the growing body like settlers fanning out from a town square. In breeds with spotting genes, some routes are blocked or some neighborhoods get their power cut, so those areas never get pigment factories at all—leaving crisp white patches. Other switches tell the factories in a region to make black, brown, or yellow, so each patch keeps its own setting and every hair in that patch shows that choice. Breeders have favored these bold patterns, so they’re common in dogs. Humans usually don’t carry such strong pattern switches, which is why most of us don’t have patchy coloring—though rare conditions like birthmarks, piebaldism, or vitiligo can create patches, showing the same principle at work.

Question: what is it that makes music in major keys sound happier and music in minor keys sound more solemn?
Answer:
At the simplest level, “major” and “minor” differ by one key ingredient: the third note of the chord or scale. Raise that note a little and you get major; lower it and you get minor. That tiny nudge changes how the notes’ vibrations line up. In a major chord, the vibrations fit together neatly—like synchronized jump ropes—so the combined sound feels smooth and bright. In a minor chord, they don’t match quite as snugly, creating a slightly rougher, darker blend. It’s the difference between clear sunlight and a thin cloud over the same scene: the picture is similar, but the mood shifts.

Your brain also reads music the way it reads voices. When people are excited or joyful, they tend to speak a bit higher, brighter, and quicker; when they’re sad, they speak lower and slower, with smaller, drooping inflections. Major music often shares the “bright, lifted” clues of happy speech, while minor music shares the “lowered, sighing” clues of sad speech—especially that lowered third, which is the musical equivalent of a vocal sigh.

Finally, we learn these meanings. Movies, lullabies, and pop songs keep pairing major with triumph and minor with wistfulness, so the association becomes as familiar as red meaning “stop.” Cultures that don’t share Western musical habits show weaker or different links between mode and emotion. So the “happy major, solemn minor” effect isn’t a single cause but a braid: physics nudges the sound toward bright or dark, the human voice provides a template our ears recognize, and culture teaches us how to name what we feel.

Question: how does a computer choose/create a random number?
Answer:
Think of a computer as an ultra‑reliable chef: given the same recipe and ingredients, it will cook the exact same dish every time. That’s great for consistency, but “randomness” is more like grabbing a handful of popcorn while your eyes are closed—unpredictable. To fake that unpredictability, computers use algorithms called pseudo‑random number generators. They start from a seed—like the first page of a very long, pre‑shuffled flipbook—and then hop deterministically from one number to the next. If you start from the same seed, you flip through the same “random‑looking” pages. This is perfect for simulations and games, where you want numbers that look jumbled, and sometimes you even want to replay the exact same jumble by reusing the seed.

When the stakes are higher—like generating passwords or encryption keys—“looks random” isn’t enough; it must be unpredictable even to someone who knows the method. Here the computer listens to the messy outside world: tiny electrical hiss in circuits, timing wiggles in hardware, disk and network delays, even the rhythm of your mouse and keyboard. The operating system collects these scraps of unpredictability into a bucket of randomness and then uses a secure mixer (a cryptographic generator) to stretch them into many high‑quality random bits. Picture tossing confetti into a sealed blender: the result is so thoroughly mixed that no one can reconstruct the original pieces.

So, when a program “chooses a random number,” it either asks a fast flipbook (seeded algorithm) or it asks the operating system’s secure blender (fed by real‑world noise). Use the flipbook when you need speed and repeatability; use the blender when you need secrecy and true unpredictability.

Question: lots of people don't feel identified or find themselves unattractive in photos. however, when they look in the mirror they usually have no problems with their image. is there a neurobiological reason for this? which image would be closer to reality as observed by a 3rd person?
Answer:
A mirror is like watching yourself on a small stage you control: you’re lit from the front, you can adjust your posture and expression in real time, and you’re seeing the version of your face you’ve seen thousands of times—left and right swapped. A photo, by contrast, is a single, unforgiving frame. It often catches you mid‑blink or mid‑word, under overhead lights that carve harsh shadows. On top of that, phone cameras use wide‑angle lenses at close range; held at arm’s length they can make your nose look larger and your ears and jaw recede, a bit like a gentle fun‑house mirror. Move the camera farther away (about 1–2 meters) with a normal lens and that distortion largely disappears.

Your brain also plays a role. It learns and prefers what it sees most—a simple “familiarity bonus.” Because you mostly see your mirror‑reversed, smoothly moving face, your visual system treats that as the “correct” template. When a photo arrives that is static, non‑reversed, and differently lit, it clashes with that internal expectation and can feel wrong. The brain also averages over motion, smoothing tiny asymmetries when you watch yourself live; a still photo freezes those asymmetries and makes them pop. Add a touch of self‑criticism, and the snapshot can seem harsher than the person others experience.

Which is closer to what a third person sees? Not the mirror (it’s flipped), and not a close‑range selfie (it’s distorted). The closest is a view from a few feet away, non‑reversed, in natural, even light—ideally in motion. In practice, a photo taken by someone else at eye level from about 1–2 meters with a normal lens, or a short video of you speaking, will best match how you look to others, who see you as a moving, expressive face rather than a single frozen moment.

Question: what is the molecular biology behind an allele being recessive or dominant?
Answer:
Think of a gene as a recipe for making a specific tool—a protein—and of each person as owning two copies of that recipe. In many jobs, having one good recipe is enough to stock the toolbox. That’s why many “broken” versions of a gene are recessive: the working copy still makes sufficient protein to keep the cell’s process above a threshold where everything looks normal. For example, if pigment production or an ion channel works fine at 50% output, a loss in one copy does not change the visible trait, so the faulty allele stays quiet in the background. This “good-enough” buffer makes most loss-of-function alleles recessive.

An allele tends to look dominant when one copy changes the system’s output despite the other copy trying to help. That can happen in three main ways. First, dose matters: some processes need close to 100% output, so one good copy can’t meet the demand; the trait shows up because the system falls below threshold (imagine running a factory line with half the workers—output drops). Second, the mutant protein can interfere with the normal one, like a warped plank in a bundle of boards ruining the whole beam; this is common when proteins work as pairs or in larger teams. Third, the mutant can act like a switch stuck “on” or “in the wrong place,” adding a new or excessive activity that the normal copy can’t counter. Classic examples map to these ideas: reduced receptor levels leading to high cholesterol (not enough dose), brittle bone from faulty collagen that spoils the fiber (teamwork spoiled), or a growth receptor that signals too much (stuck-on switch). In short, “dominant” and “recessive” aren’t battles between alleles; they reflect whether one good copy keeps the cellular machine above its performance threshold and whether the altered protein merely reduces output or actively rewires, jams, or overdrives the system.

Question: if photons travel along waves with varying frequencies, but these waves all traverse distance at the same speed (c), then are the photons in higher frequency waves, which would be longer, traveling faster?
Answer:
Short answer: no. In empty space, all photons move at the same speed, the speed of light c. What changes with color (frequency) is the spacing between the wave crests, not the speed. Frequency (how many crests pass each second) times wavelength (the distance between crests) must equal the speed. So if the frequency is higher, the wavelength must be shorter, keeping the product equal to c.

Picture cars all cruising at the same highway speed. The “rumble strips” on the road are the wave crests. If a driver feels more bumps per second (higher frequency), it’s because the strips are closer together (shorter wavelength), not because the car sped up. Photons in higher-frequency light (like blue) aren’t “longer” and they don’t travel faster; they just carry more energy per photon than lower-frequency light (like red). One footnote: in materials like glass or water, different colors can propagate at slightly different effective speeds because of interactions with the medium, but in a vacuum they all move at c.

Question: why is anything radioactive in movies, portrayed as a green glow?
Answer:
Because filmmakers need a quick visual shorthand. Green reads as eerie and “not of nature,” especially in the dark. Our eyes are most sensitive to green light, so a small amount of it looks bright and spooky on camera—like a highlighter scrawled across a night scene. History also primed us: 19th‑century “poison greens” (arsenic‑based pigments) gave the color a toxic reputation, comic books turned “radiation” into green-skinned heroes and slime, and early glow‑in‑the‑dark paints and plastics often glowed green because that’s the easiest, most efficient color for common phosphors to emit. Put those together and green became the movie world’s “hazard” color, much like a skull-and-crossbones for light.

In real life, most radioactive stuff does not glow. When you do see glow connected to radiation, it’s usually because the radiation is making something else light up: old radium watch dials used a radioactive source to excite a phosphor that emits green light; uranium glass looks green under ultraviolet light for the same reason; and nuclear reactor pools famously shine—not green but an icy blue—due to a different effect called Cherenkov radiation. So the green glow is part truth filtered through prop paint, human vision, and pop culture, solidified into a cinematic cue: show green, think “radiation.”

Question: when you freeze and thaw fruit, it turns to mush. if you froze/thawed your hand, it would turn black and die. but if you freeze/thaw steak and other things, they remain juicy and perfectly fine. why do some things freeze "well" but not others?
Answer:
Think of cells as tiny water balloons. Fruit is a field of thin‑skinned balloons packed with watery juice; when you freeze it slowly (like in a home freezer), ice crystals grow large and act like little knives, puncturing those balloons. When it thaws, the walls are torn and the juice leaks out, so the fruit slumps into mush. Meat, by contrast, is built more like bundles of ropes (protein fibers) threaded with some water and fat. Even if some balloons in meat pop and some liquid drips out when thawing, the ropey scaffold stays intact, so steak still feels like steak rather than pudding.

Two other things decide whether something “freezes well”: speed and recipe. Fast freezing makes many tiny crystals that do less damage—this is why flash‑frozen peas stay snappy while the same peas frozen slowly at home get mealy. Ingredients that tie up water—sugars, salts, fats, and gels like pectin or gelatin—also keep crystals small and limit damage. Ice cream is the poster child: sugar and fat keep water from forming big crystals, and churning adds air, so it thaws creamy. Watery, delicate tissues with big, taut cells—lettuce, cucumbers, many berries—lack those protections and collapse after thawing.

A living hand adds a harsher problem: it’s not just texture, it’s survival. Freezing forms ice both in and around cells, but it also freezes the blood, clogging tiny vessels. Cells are crushed and dehydrated by ice, and when you thaw, damaged vessels leak and clots block flow, so tissue starves of oxygen and dies—turning black like a frost‑burnt leaf. A steak doesn’t need blood flow anymore; its structure only has to be pleasant to chew, not alive, so it can weather freezing with far less drama.

Question: panthalassa was the giant, planet wide, ocean surrounding pangaea. what effects would a giant ocean have on the weather?
Answer:
Imagine the planet wrapped in one vast bathtub. Water warms and cools slowly, so a giant ocean acts like a thermal flywheel: it mutes temperature swings over the sea and feeds the air with moisture. Over Panthalassa itself, weather would tend to be steadier—fewer wild day‑to‑day temperature jumps, long rolling swells, and broad belts of rain where warm, moist air rises near the equator. With no continents to interrupt them, storms could organize over great distances; once a tropical cyclone formed, it could wander and survive much longer because there’s no land to cut off its fuel, though whether they formed often would still depend on winds and water temperatures at the time. Ocean currents—huge, simple gyres like slow‑moving rivers—would sweep heat around the globe, softening cold at some high latitudes and preventing the tropics from getting quite as hot over open water.

Now place Pangaea like a massive rock in that bathtub. The coastlines would be stormy and very wet in warm seasons, because hot land sucks in ocean air the way a blacktop parking lot draws a summer breeze; think “mega‑monsoons” that drench the margins, then reverse to dry, offshore winds in cooler seasons. But the supercontinent’s deep interior would be far from the ocean’s moisture and its temperature‑balancing touch. There, weather would swing to extremes: scorching, dusty summers and bitter, dry winters, with vast deserts because rain simply runs out of steam long before reaching the middle. In short, the giant ocean would smooth and moisten the world over water and coasts, while the sheer size of the neighboring land would sharpen contrasts at the shoreline and leave the heart of the continent harsh and dry.

Question: in order to calculate relative atomic mass the masses of isotopes have to be taken into account. how did the scientists know (initially) what is the abundance of those isotopes?
Answer:
The first hint came from simple weighing. Chemists noticed that some elements did not have whole‑number atomic weights: chlorine, for example, averaged about 35.45. That odd number suggested a mix of two kinds of chlorine atoms—one near 35 and one near 37—blended in fixed proportions. In 1913, J. J. Thomson actually saw two kinds of neon atoms by bending a beam of charged neon atoms (ions) in electric and magnetic fields: two distinct traces appeared, one heavier than the other. This showed isotopes exist, but scientists still needed a way to measure “how much of each.”

Francis Aston solved that with the mass spectrograph, a device that acts like a prism for atoms. You send a stream of charged atoms through electric and magnetic fields; lighter ones curve more, heavier ones less, so they land at different spots on a photographic plate. The darker each spot, the more atoms of that isotope hit there. After correcting for the instrument’s sensitivity (a simple calibration, like zeroing a scale), the relative darkness—or, in modern instruments, the peak height—gives the natural abundance. Chlorine shows two spots in about a 3:1 ratio, matching ~75% chlorine‑35 and ~25% chlorine‑37, which averages to the familiar 35.45. Later, improved mass spectrometers refined these numbers, and for radioactive isotopes scientists could also count decays, but the core idea has remained the same: split the isotopes, then compare how many arrive.

Question: is it true that animals with more types of color receptive cones can see colors we cannot conceive of?
Answer:
Short answer: often yes, with caveats. Color is your brain’s best guess after comparing signals from different kinds of light‑sensing cells called cones. Humans have three types, so our “color mixer” has three sliders. Many birds, reptiles, and fish add a fourth slider (often sensitive to ultraviolet), giving them an extra independent way to compare light. That extra channel expands their color space the way adding a new axis expands a map into a globe. With four sliders you can mix shades—like “UV‑red” or “UV‑green” blends—that our three‑slider system can’t reproduce or even imagine as a genuine experience.

A practical consequence is that these animals can tell apart light mixtures that look identical to us. Two different spectra may collapse into the same human color but separate cleanly for a tetrachromat. That’s why flowers and feathers carry UV patterns that are invisible to us but glaring billboards to a bird. We can make false‑color photos that assign UV to a visible tint, but that’s only a translation, not the original sensation.

The caveat: more cone types don’t automatically mean “better” color in every sense. The mantis shrimp famously has many receptor types, yet seems to compare them less, so its color discrimination isn’t as fine as you might think. Wiring matters as much as parts. Also, a small fraction of humans may have a fourth cone variant and report extra shade differences. Bottom line: many animals with more cone types likely perceive hues we cannot experience, even if we can describe them mathematically—we just don’t have the extra slider to feel them.

Question: what was the weather/climate like during pangea?
Answer:
Pangea was a single supercontinent that stretched almost from pole to pole about 335–175 million years ago. Because so much land was clumped together, huge areas lay far from the ocean—the planet’s natural air conditioner. Imagine a continent the size of all today’s continents fused, with a stark, sunbaked interior and more moderate edges. The result was sharp seasonal swings: very hot summers and cold winters inland, with vast deserts and sand seas like Sahara-on-steroids. Along the coasts and near big mountain belts, seasonal wind reversals (monsoons) pumped moisture on and off the land, bringing months of heavy rain followed by long dry spells. Mountains also cast “rain shadows,” leaving one side wet and the other parched.

Climate wasn’t the same for all of Pangea’s lifetime. Early on, during the late Carboniferous and early Permian, the far-southern part carried large ice sheets, while the equatorial belt was humid enough to grow swampy forests that later became coal. As time moved into the Permian and Triassic, the world warmed, polar ice retreated, and the supercontinent’s interior became even drier and hotter, building immense dune fields and salt flats. Meanwhile, the coastal zones experienced a super-sized monsoon pattern that drenched them seasonally. Even the high latitudes were milder than today at times, supporting forests and animals near the poles. In short: Pangea’s weather was continental and extreme at its heart, monsoonal around its edges, and it shifted from icy-and-humid belts to predominantly warm-and-dry as the supercontinent aged.

Question: if we travel 65 million light years, we would be able to see the extinction of dinosaurs, but how is that possible and why?
Answer:
Think of light as the Universe’s mail service: every moment, Earth sends out “postcards” of how it looks, and those postcards travel at the speed of light. The farther you stand from Earth, the older the postcards that are just arriving. So if you could magically teleport to a spot 65 million light‑years away and point a fantastically powerful telescope back at Earth, the light reaching you there left our planet 65 million years ago. You wouldn’t be seeing Earth “now”; you’d be opening very old mail— snapshots from the time of the dinosaurs. This time-delay is the same reason you see a lightning bolt before you hear the thunder, just stretched to cosmic scales.

In practice, several caveats matter. You can’t get there faster than light, so traveling to that vantage point would itself take at least 65 million years. Even if you could teleport, Earth would be a tiny, faint dot from that distance; resolving individual dinosaurs is beyond any plausible telescope. However, the extinction event itself—an enormous impact in what’s now the Yucatán—might show up in principle as a brief, bright flash, followed by months to years of a dust-dimmed, smoke-hazed Earth whose reflected light changes noticeably. So the “how and why” boil down to one simple fact: light takes time, and distance is a time machine. The farther you look, the further back you’re peeking into our planet’s home movie.

Question: why are there so few elements that are liquid at room temperature?
Answer:
Imagine each element as a crowd of people on a dance floor. Their “glue” for sticking together is the attraction between their particles; the “shake” that tries to pull them apart is the jiggling from heat. If the glue easily beats the shake, you get a rigid crowd: a solid. If the shake wins, everyone flies apart: a gas. A liquid is the narrow middle ground where people stay together but can still slide past each other. At room temperature, the shake is moderate, so only elements with just-right-strength glue land in that middle zone. Most elements have glue that’s too strong (they’re solids), and a few have glue that’s too weak (they’re gases), so only a couple happen to be liquids.

Why those couple? Bromine is made of fairly heavy, two-atom molecules. Being heavy gives them more “stickiness” to each other than lighter gases like chlorine, but not so much that they lock rigidly—perfect for a liquid near room temperature. Mercury is the opposite story: as a metal, you’d expect strong bonding, but its inner electrons move so fast (a consequence of being a very heavy atom) that its outer electrons don’t bind neighbors very effectively. The metal “glue” is unusually weak, so mercury melts so low that it’s liquid in your thermometer.

There are near misses that show the idea. Gallium melts in a warm hand, and cesium melts on a hot day; rubidium isn’t far off. Change the room—say, make “room temperature” 40°C or 10°C—and the list of liquid elements would change. So the scarcity isn’t a deep rule of nature; it’s mostly that the Goldilocks window for being liquid at our everyday temperature is small, and only a few elements happen to sit in it.

Question: there is a bird inside a large cargo plane. does the plane weigh less if the bird flies inside the plane?
Answer:
Short answer: no. In a closed cargo plane, the total weight is the same whether the bird is perching or flying. When the bird flies, its wings push air downward. That moving air then pushes on the floor and walls of the plane, passing the bird’s weight to the plane through the air, like a tiny helicopter using the cabin air as a conveyor belt for force. So the scale under the plane still “feels” bird plus plane.

There are brief wiggles. When the bird takes off or lands, the push on the air changes quickly, so the plane’s weight reading can momentarily dip or spike. And if the cabin were very leaky so the downwash escaped outside, a small difference could appear while air is being blown out. But in a typical sealed cargo bay and during steady flapping, the average weight is unchanged—the air inside simply carries the bird’s weight to the airplane’s structure.

Question: why do beavers build dams?
Answer:
Beavers build dams for the same reasons a family might raise the floor of their house and dig a moat: safety, stability, and easy access to supplies. By stacking sticks and mud across a stream, they slow the current and create a pond. In that deeper, quieter water they place their lodge, which has an underwater front door. Predators like coyotes or bears can’t easily swim down to it, but a beaver can slip in like a diver heading home. The pond also lets them float heavy branches instead of dragging them, and it keeps a pantry of twigs cached underwater near the lodge for winter meals. Just as important, the dam keeps water levels steady when streams rise and fall, so the door stays submerged and the pantry stays reachable. Beavers even “listen” for the sound of running water and plug leaks, like a handyman chasing a hiss of air to find a tire puncture.

Not every beaver needs a dam; in big rivers or natural lakes where water is already deep and stable, they may simply dig bank dens or build lodges without damming. But where streams are shallow, their dams transform trickles into wetlands—spongy, life-rich places that slow floods, store water for droughts, trap sediment, cool the area, and provide homes for fish, frogs, birds, and insects. Sometimes this floods roads or trees, so people use flow devices to share the water. In short, a dam is a beaver’s way of remodeling the neighborhood to fit its needs—and in doing so, this small “civil engineer” ends up shaping an entire landscape.

Question: are we aware of any linguistic differences between the korean spoken in north and south korea that have developed since the end of the korean war?
what do nocturnal insects such as cockroaches do during the day?
Answer:
Think of nocturnal insects as night-shift workers. When the sun is up, they clock out and retreat to safe “break rooms” — narrow cracks, under bark or stones, deep leaf litter, or the gaps behind kitchen appliances. These spots are dark, tight, and a little humid, which helps them hide from daytime hunters like birds and lizards and prevents them from drying out; small bodies lose water fast. By day they keep activity to a minimum, guided by an internal daily timer (a circadian rhythm) that tells them it’s rest time until dusk. If a place is dark enough — like a sewer or a deep cupboard — they might still move about, but in general they lie low and conserve energy.

Cockroaches follow this pattern closely. They huddle together in shelters marked by their own scent cues, a kind of “Vacancy: Safe Here” sign that draws others to the same refuge. While holed up, they do quiet maintenance: digest last night’s meal, groom their antennae and legs to keep their “sensors” clean, and sometimes molt in safety. Females may also guard or carry egg cases while hidden. If you flip on a light and see them scatter, that’s their alarm: bright, open spaces mean danger. Only when evening returns do they head out to forage, court, and explore, resuming the night shift.

Question: could a solar flare destroy mercury?
Answer:
If you mean the planet Mercury: no. A solar flare is a sudden flash of light and a blast of fast-moving particles from the Sun. They are dramatic—like the Sun sneezing glitter and wind at the same time—but they spread out as they travel. Even at Mercury’s close orbit, a flare can heat the surface a bit, jostle its tiny, patchy magnetic shield, and sandblast a few atoms off the topmost rock. Think of it as a gritty breeze scuffing paint, not a bomb shattering a stone. The planet’s bulk stays intact.

To actually tear a planet apart you’d need energy on the scale of its own gravity holding it together—far beyond what our Sun’s flares can deliver. Over very long times, Mercury will change for other reasons: micrometeorite impacts, gradual loss of surface atoms to space, and, in billions of years, the Sun swelling into a red giant that may engulf it. But no single flare, or even a big series of them, can “destroy” the planet.

If you meant the metal mercury (the silvery liquid) here on Earth: also no. Solar flares can disturb radio signals, trigger beautiful auroras, and bother satellites, but Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field are a sturdy umbrella. They stop the harmful stuff from reaching the ground in amounts that could vaporize or “erase” a substance. An element can be heated, moved, or ionized, but not annihilated by a flare; a puddle of mercury isn’t going to vanish because the Sun burped.

Question: if something was on fire in a fridge that could go to extremely low temperatures and it kept getting colder. is there a lower temperature limit where the fire can no longer exist?
Answer:
Fire is a self-sustaining chemical reaction that needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to keep the reaction going. Think of the flame as a runner who has to stay warm to keep moving. Put that runner in a freezer that keeps getting colder, and the cold steals heat faster than the runner can make it. At some point the flame can no longer keep its thin, hot reaction zone warm, and it “stalls” and goes out. This cut-off isn’t a single magic temperature for all fires; it depends on the fuel, how big the flame is, and how quickly the surroundings pull heat away. Small flames on cold metal, for example, are quenched easily; big bonfires can survive in snow because they make and retain enough heat. Fuels also have a lowest temperature at which they give off enough vapor to burn; cool them below that and the flame starves.

If you keep cooling to extreme temperatures, there is an absolute wall: the oxygen in the air itself stops being a gas. At normal pressure, oxygen liquefies at about −183°C (−297°F). Below that, there’s essentially no gaseous oxygen to feed a flame, so combustion cannot continue no matter what the fuel is. Long before you reach that point, though, most fires in a super-cold, highly heat-sucking “fridge” would already have been snuffed out by a mix of insufficient fuel vapor, slowed reaction rates, and relentless heat loss.

Question: when a rocket needs to restart its engines in space, what makes sure the fuel is where it needs to be?
Answer:
In weightlessness, fuel doesn’t “settle” at the bottom of a tank—it floats like glitter in a snow globe. If a rocket tried to restart like that, its engine might suck gas instead of liquid, much like a straw slurping air at the end of a drink. To gather the fuel where the plumbing can grab it, rockets do a quick nudge called a settling or ullage burn: small thrusters fire briefly to give the vehicle a gentle push. That tiny acceleration makes the fuel drift “down” toward the tank outlet, creating a clear pool of liquid for the engine to draw from.

Inside the tanks, designers also add simple but clever guides that work with this gentle push. Think of vanes, screens, and sponge-like meshes that use surface tension to herd liquid into a corner, channels that lead it to the pickup, or flexible bladders/diaphragms that keep fuel and gas separated. The tanks are also pressurized—often with helium—so the liquid is pushed toward the engine like toothpaste in a squeezed tube. Sometimes the whole stage is slowly spun so “centrifugal gravity” keeps the fuel pinned outward. Together—settling thrust, smart tank internals, and steady pressurization—make sure the engine sees only liquid when it’s time to light again.

Question: are there any mammals with the same or similar vocal range/abilities as humans?
Answer:
It helps to separate two ideas: how high or low an animal can pitch its voice (vocal range), and how flexibly it can shape sounds into something speech-like (vocal ability). Humans are unusual because we combine a versatile “instrument” (lungs, voice box, tongue, lips) with a very skilled “conductor” (fine brain control and learning). That lets us rapidly switch between many distinct sounds and stitch them into words and sentences.

Some mammals can do striking parts of this. Seals and sea lions are the best mammalian mimics of human-like sounds: trained individuals can copy the melody and rhythm of phrases, and harbor seals can shape their mouth and throat to produce vowel-like patterns; a famous example is “Hoover,” a harbor seal that imitated human speechy phrases. Whales and dolphins cover enormous pitch ranges and can learn new calls; a beluga nicknamed NOC produced underwater sounds that fooled divers into thinking a person was talking nearby. But cetaceans make sounds with nasal structures rather than a voice box and tongue, so they don’t carve out crisp consonants and vowels the way we do.

Others add more pieces to the puzzle. Elephants boom at the low end and one Asian elephant, Koshik, copied several Korean words by putting his trunk in his mouth to reshape sounds. Bats reach the high end and some species learn new call patterns, a bit like local “dialects.” Nonhuman primates have vocal tracts that could, in theory, make many human-like sounds, but they lack the fine voluntary control to do it on command. In short, no other mammal matches the full human package of range plus speech-ready control, but different groups each hold a shard of the mirror: whales for span, seals for mimicry, elephants for the bass notes, and bats for the treble—humans uniquely blend them into language.

Question: what do we experience when we hear a soundwave that is very loud ( > 150db) but also outside of the hearing range?
Answer:
“Outside the hearing range” means the sound’s pitch is too low (infrasound, below about 20 Hz) or too high (ultrasound, above about 20 kHz) for us to hear as a tone. But a very large sound pressure, like 150 dB, still shoves on your body the way a strong wind moves a door, whether or not you hear it. So instead of “hearing” it, you feel it. Infrasound at that level can feel like a slow ocean swell rolling through you: pressure in the ears, a flutter in the chest or abdomen, dizziness, nausea, and a sense of unease. Your eyes and skin may vibrate slightly, your vision can blur, and nearby objects may rattle and buzz, creating regular audible noises even if the original wave is inaudible.

Ultrasound that strong is more like an invisible sandblaster of tiny pressure taps. You typically don’t hear a pitch, but you may feel ear fullness, a hot or tingling sensation on the skin, a headache, or dizziness. Extremely intense ultrasound and infrasound can also “leak” into the audible world indirectly: they can make parts of your head or nearby surfaces vibrate and produce lower, hearable by‑products, so you might notice faint tones or buzzes. At 150 dB, both kinds can cause harm—temporary or permanent ear damage, and, if higher still, even tissue injury—so the experience can quickly shift from odd and uncomfortable to painful and dangerous, even though no clear “sound” is heard.

Question: if you were to put a chunk of coal at the deepest part of the ocean, would it turn into a diamond?
Answer:
Short answer: no. Diamonds do not come from coal, and the deepest ocean is nowhere near the right “workshop” to make them. Most natural diamonds formed far beneath continents, in the Earth’s mantle, long before the first forests ever existed. Coal comes from plants buried near the surface; diamonds come from carbon that was cooked and squeezed deep below, then carried up by volcanic eruptions. So the coal-to-diamond idea is a popular mix‑up.

Now imagine two machines. The deepest ocean is a gigantic refrigerator with a gentle squeeze: very cold, and about 1,100 times the pressure of air at sea level. Diamond-making needs a roaring forge with a crushing grip: roughly 40–50 times more pressure than the deepest trench and temperatures around 900–1,300°C. So dropping coal into the Mariana Trench is like putting bread dough in a freezer and hoping it bakes into a loaf—wrong place, wrong conditions.

What would actually happen to the coal? It would get waterlogged, colonized by microbes, slowly crumble, and be buried by sediment. Only if that carbon were later dragged deep into the Earth by plate tectonics and heated and squeezed for millions of years might some of it join the mantle’s diamond-making cycle—and by then it wouldn’t be a chunk of coal anymore. The ocean floor itself won’t turn coal into diamond; it’s the mantle’s hidden forge that does.

Question: why do i wake up 5-10 minutes before my alarm?
Answer:
Your brain keeps time. If you wake up at about the same hour each day, your “internal clock” learns the pattern and starts the wake‑up sequence before the alarm rings. Think of a theater: a few minutes before the curtain rises, the stage crew brings up the house lights and the orchestra tunes. In your body, wake‑promoting signals like a rise in body temperature, a small bump in heart rate, and a surge of the “get‑going” hormone cortisol start to nudge you toward the surface of sleep. That gentle preheating makes the alarm less jarring, and sometimes you pop awake a few minutes early.

Sleep also runs in cycles, like laps in a pool, each about 90 minutes. You’re more likely to wake spontaneously at the end of a lap, when sleep is lighter. If one of those natural endpoints lands near your usual alarm time, small cues—morning light leaking around the curtains, a neighbor’s car door, a full bladder, or even the quiet expectancy of “don’t oversleep!”—can tip you into wakefulness right before the buzzer. If you wake a bit early and feel refreshed, it’s a sign your clock is well tuned. If you’re waking much earlier than planned, feel anxious or unrefreshed, or it starts to affect your days, try tightening your routine (consistent bed/wake times, bright light in the morning, a dark cool bedroom at night), or check in with a clinician to rule out stress, caffeine timing, or a sleep disorder.

Question: why does waking up with an alarm make you feel more tired then waking up naturally even if the time you woke up naturally is before the alarm?
Answer:
Think of waking up like coming to the surface from underwater. When you wake naturally, your body is already swimming upward: your internal clock has started to raise body temperature, lower melatonin, and release a small burst of cortisol that acts like a gentle tow to the surface. You’re usually at a lighter part of a sleep cycle, so breaking the surface feels smooth. An alarm, by contrast, is a sudden yank on your ankle. It can pull you up from deeper sleep or vivid dreaming, and that abruptness triggers a mini stress response. The result is sleep inertia—your brain’s “sleep brakes” are still on—so thinking, mood, and coordination lag for a while.

This also explains why you can feel worse even if your natural wake time is earlier than the alarm. If you wake up on your own and then roll over “just for a few more minutes,” you can drop back into a deeper stage, so the alarm rips you out of heavier sleep than the moment you first woke. Snoozing repeats the problem. If you naturally surface before the alarm, getting up then often feels best—you’ve caught the wave at the right moment. In short: smooth ascent (natural wake) beats emergency winch (alarm), not because of the clock time, but because of where you are in the sleep cycle and how gently you transition to wakefulness.

Question: why do people with down syndrome seem to look very similar to each other facially/stature despite their families looking different?
Answer:
People with Down syndrome share certain facial features and body build because they share the same underlying change in their instruction manual: an extra copy of chromosome 21. Think of chromosomes as pages in a recipe book for building a person. If one page is copied three times instead of two, the ingredients on that page are all added a little more than usual. This “extra dose” doesn’t break the recipe, but it nudges growth in consistent directions during early development. So across many families, the same patterns tend to appear, much like loaves baked from the same recipe with one ingredient slightly over-measured will all rise and shape in a similar way.

Those “nudges” affect how the skull, face, and skeleton form, and how firm muscles and connective tissues are. The midface often grows a bit flatter, the nasal bridge lower, the eyes can appear more almond-shaped, and the tongue may seem larger relative to the mouth; lower muscle tone softens facial expressions and posture, and bones tend to grow to a shorter average height. Because the same set of instructions is turned up across all people with Down syndrome, these features repeat, sometimes strongly enough to outweigh usual family resemblance. Still, there is plenty of individual variation: not everyone has the same features to the same degree, some people have mosaic forms with fewer cells carrying the extra chromosome, and family traits do show through. In short, a shared chromosomal change creates a shared look, while each person’s unique genetics and life shape the details.

Question: has the increase in size of hard drives stagnated? why?
Answer:
Short answer: growth has slowed, not stopped. In the 2000s, hard‑drive space felt like a balloon inflating every year; now it’s more like a slow, steady breath. Top capacities crept from about 10 TB in the mid‑2010s to the mid‑20s by the mid‑2020s, with the first 30‑plus‑terabyte models just arriving. That’s progress, but at roughly 5–15% per year instead of the old “double every couple of years” pace.

The main brake is physics. A hard drive stores data as tiny magnetic “grains” on spinning disks. To fit more data, you squeeze those grains closer and make each one smaller—like building houses closer and thinner on the same street. Past a point, the walls get so thin that a warm breeze (ordinary heat) can flip a grain’s direction and scramble the data. To keep writing reliably at those sizes, manufacturers need tricks like briefly heating the spot they write to or nudging it with microwaves. These methods work, but they’re hard to engineer at scale and to keep reliable for years. On top of that, the size of the disks and the number you can stack in a 3.5‑inch case are basically fixed; adding more platters runs into vibration, power, and heat limits, even with helium‑filled drives. Economics matters too: only a few companies make hard drives now, and their biggest customers (cloud data centers) care most about cost per terabyte and reliability, so the industry favors careful, incremental gains. Net result: capacities are still rising, but in measured steps, not leaps.

Question: is it a coincidence that all elements are present on earth?
Answer:
Short answer: it’s not a coincidence. The elements on Earth are the leftovers of earlier generations of stars. Think of the universe as a series of cosmic foundries: small stars made the light elements, giant stars forged many of the heavier ones in their cores, and spectacular events like supernovae and neutron-star mergers sprinkled space with the rest. Our Sun and planets formed from this mixed “stellar dust.” As Earth assembled, it acted like a giant sorting machine: light gases (like hydrogen and much helium) mostly escaped, iron-loving metals sank to the core, and heat drove off some volatile stuff near the young Sun. What remained became the Earth’s crust, oceans, and air—carrying along a sampler of many elements created long before Earth existed.

That said, not every element is naturally present in practical amounts. Nearly all elements up to uranium can be found on Earth, but a few (such as technetium and promethium) have no long-lived versions, so they appear only in vanishingly tiny, short-lived traces made by natural nuclear reactions. Heavier-than-uranium elements are mostly made by us in laboratories, with only rare, fleeting natural occurrences. So Earth’s elemental lineup isn’t random; it’s a predictable result of how stars build elements, how some decay away with time, and how our planet kept or lost materials during its fiery youth.

Question: as bananas emit small amounts of gamma radiation, would it be theoretically possible to get radiation sickness/poisoning in a room completely full of them?
do human vocal cords produce sounds outside the range of human hearing?
Answer:
Short answer: not really above it, a little bit below it. Human hearing spans roughly 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. Your vocal cords work like a tiny, fast camera shutter, opening and closing to make a buzzing source that the mouth and throat then shape into vowels and add hiss for consonants. In everyday speech this buzzing is around 80–250 hertz for most adults, higher for children and some singers, and the hiss of sounds like “s” and “sh” reaches into the high thousands of hertz—but stays within the normal hearing band.

At the edges, two special cases appear. On the low side, “vocal fry” is like slow popcorn popping: the pulses can drop toward 20 hertz, brushing the bottom limit of hearing. At that point you tend to feel a rumble more than hear a clear tone, so there can be a small infrasound component. On the high side, the cords cannot flap anywhere near ultrasonic rates, and while any buzz produces faint overtones that march upward, those above 20,000 hertz are vanishingly weak and effectively absent in normal speech or singing. So the human voice doesn’t meaningfully produce ultrasound, but it can flirt with infrasound when used in very low, creaky registers.

Question: how does gravity create energy?
Answer:
Gravity doesn’t create energy; it rearranges it. Think of gravity as a giant slide built into the universe. When you put a ball on a high shelf, you’ve “paid in” energy by lifting it. Let it go, and gravity simply lets that stored energy (gravitational potential energy) flow into motion (kinetic energy). When the ball hits the ground, that motion becomes heat and sound. A dam works the same way: sunlight evaporates water, weather lifts it to mountains (the “deposit”), and as water falls through turbines, gravity helps convert that stored height into electricity. Gravity is like a careful banker moving funds between accounts—never minting new money.

On grander scales, gravity’s bookkeeping powers entire cosmic engines. When gas clouds collapse under their own weight, the fall converts potential energy into heat, making the gas glow and, in stars, helping them get hot enough for fusion—gravity sets the stage; fusion provides the ongoing fire. Matter spiraling into a neutron star or black hole heats up dramatically; the light from quasars is powered by this gravitational “fall.” Even ripples in spacetime—gravitational waves from merging black holes—carry away energy that comes from the pair’s orbital energy, leaving the final object with a bit less mass. In all these cases, energy isn’t created out of nothing; gravity provides the downhill path that lets stored energy turn into other forms.

Question: could an asteroid hit earth at an angle that caused the earth to spin significantly faster or slower? what effect would that have on us?
Answer:
Picture Earth as a spinning top and an asteroid as a thrown pebble. To change the top’s spin, you must hit near the rim and push with or against the spin. Likewise, an asteroid would need to strike near Earth’s equator, moving east-to-west to slow us or west-to-east to speed us up; a strike near the poles mostly tilts the axis rather than changing the spin rate. The catch is scale. Even the dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impactor (about 10 km wide) likely changed the length of the day by only a few milliseconds—too small to notice without precise instruments. To change Earth’s spin by even 1% (about 15 minutes per day), you’d need something roughly the size and mass of a small dwarf planet hitting in just the right way. That’s the sort of blow associated with moon-forming events, not routine asteroids.

What would it do to us? For the small, realistic changes (milliseconds), essentially nothing beyond the usual climate and geological chaos of a large impact itself. For a big change, the impact would be globally catastrophic long before the altered day length mattered. Still, imagine the hypothetical aftermath if the planet somehow survived: a faster-spinning Earth would have shorter days, stronger winds and jet streams (the atmosphere “leans” harder into the turn), and a fatter equatorial bulge that pulls ocean water toward the equator, raising sea level there and lowering it near the poles. A slower-spinning Earth would lengthen days and nights, amplifying daytime heat and nighttime cold, and would weaken those winds. Any off-axis hit could also tilt the planet, rewriting the map of seasons. In short, the angle does matter—but the kind of impact that could noticeably change our spin is so enormous that its immediate effects would overshadow the new timetable it sets.

Question: concerning hair color, how is it that there are blondes, browns, blacks, reds, etc., but no blue, pink and other colors like that?
Answer:
Human hair is colored by just two natural pigments, both forms of melanin. Think of each hair as a clear glass filament with tiny grains sprinkled inside. Eumelanin makes brown-to-black grains (like coffee grounds), and pheomelanin makes yellow-to-red grains (like paprika). How much of each is added, and how finely they’re spread, gives the familiar range: lots of eumelanin makes black, less makes brown, very little makes blond; more pheomelanin pushes the color toward red. When the follicle stops adding pigment, the “glass” grows clear and the hair looks gray or white.

Why no blues, greens, or hot pinks? Because humans (and mammals in general) only load hair with melanin; we don’t make blue or pink hair pigments. Animals that look blue or neon often use different tricks: birds and butterflies create “structural colors,” tiny orderly layers that bounce light like a peacock’s feather or a soap bubble, or they pack in other pigments such as carotenoids that can make flamingos pink. Human hair lacks both the special pigments and the precise nanoscale layering needed to produce those colors. At most, very dark hair can look a bit bluish in the shine, and swimmers can pick up a green tint from copper in pools—but those are surface effects, not built-in color.

Question: how do parrots (and other birds that can talk) make labial sounds like f or b if they don’t have flexible lips?
Answer:
Parrots aren’t pronouncing letters the way we do; they’re impressionists matching the sound our ears expect. Instead of flexible lips and a vibrating larynx, they use a special voice box deep in the chest called the syrinx, perched where the windpipe splits. Think of the syrinx like a tiny, very controllable reed instrument: it can start and stop airflow quickly, change pitch, and add a buzz. Up in the mouth, a parrot’s thick, agile tongue and the gap between the beak halves act like adjustable doors and tunnels that shape that buzz. By coordinating these parts, the bird sculpts the same acoustic cues your brain labels as “f,” “b,” and friends—even if the “machinery” is totally different.

For pop-like sounds such as “b” or “p,” the bird briefly blocks the airstream (mainly at the syrinx) and then releases it, creating a little burst; if it keeps the buzz going through that burst, you hear something closer to “b,” if not, it leans toward “p.” For hissy sounds like “f” or “v,” it forces air through a very narrow gap—between tongue and beak or the beak tips—so the air turns turbulent, like the whoosh of a leaky bike tire; add buzz from the syrinx and the hiss becomes a “v.” The beak opening also tunes the mouth cavity, much like moving your hands over a bottle’s opening changes its note, helping fine‑shape the sound. The result isn’t a perfect copy of human articulation, but it’s close enough that our ears “round off” the differences—much as we recognize a melody whether it’s played on a flute or whistled.

Question: why is it recommended to completely finish an oral antibiotic prescription, while topical antibiotics (ex. polysporin and other antibiotic creams) can be applied as needed?
Answer:
Think of oral antibiotics like turning on a sprinkler system to water the whole yard: the medicine goes everywhere through your bloodstream to reach germs that may be scattered deep in tissues and organs. To fully clear them, the drug has to stay at a bacteria-killing level for a set number of days. If you stop early because you feel better, you’ve only cut down the “easy” germs; the tougher stragglers can bounce back and may become harder to treat next time. That’s why the plan is usually “finish as prescribed,” so the last hidden pockets are dealt with, not just the ones that were making the most noise.

Topical antibiotics are more like a spot-spray on a weed growing in a crack in the sidewalk: you can put a very high dose right where the problem is, with little exposure to the rest of the body. For small, surface problems, that direct hit is often enough for a short time, and many minor cuts don’t need antibiotic creams at all—cleaning and covering are usually best. When a topical is used, it’s typically applied for a few days and then stopped once the skin is clearly healing. “As needed” doesn’t mean “whenever forever,” though—overusing creams can still lead to resistant skin bacteria and allergic rashes. In short: systemic infections need a full, timed course to clear hidden holdouts; small surface issues can often be treated briefly—or not require antibiotics at all—guided by the product directions or your clinician’s advice.

Question: how does hypnotism actually work?
Answer:
Think of hypnosis as switching your mind from a floodlight to a spotlight. Instead of scanning everything, your attention narrows, daydreaming deepens, and you become more willing to test out ideas the guide suggests—like turning up or down the “volume knobs” on pain, anxiety, or habit urges. It’s not sleep and not mind control. People stay aware, but they’re absorbed—like getting lost in a movie. This effect comes from a blend of focused attention, vivid imagination, and expectation (“this will help”), plus the social pact of cooperating with the hypnotist. Some people are naturally more “absorbable” than others, so they respond more strongly. Inductions (soft voice, breathing, imagery) mainly serve to quiet distractions and set the stage for suggestions to land.

Under the hood, brain scans show a shift in how control and feeling systems talk to each other. Frontal “coach” areas that set goals link more tightly with regions that flag what matters, while the self-chatter network quiets down. That combination makes imagined experiences feel more real and lets suggestions steer perception and attention—hence lab findings like reduced pain, altered color or taste experiences, and even fewer errors on tricky word-color tasks. Hypnosis works best for things the brain can modulate—pain, anxiety, some habits, irritable bowel symptoms—and as a partner to standard treatments, not a solo miracle. It can’t make you do what you firmly oppose, and it doesn’t create perfect playback of memories. In short, hypnosis is a cooperative state of focused imagination that lets the brain’s control systems retune how experiences are built.

how can one actually "waste" water?
Answer:
You can’t destroy water, but you can waste usable freshwater. Think of your local supply as a library of clean books. If you borrow a book and return it to the same shelf, others can read it; if you spill coffee on it or mail it to another city, your town has one fewer copy. Water is “wasted” when we make it unavailable where and when people and ecosystems need it. Examples include letting a tap run or leaking pipes send drinking-quality water down the drain; watering lawns at noon so much of it evaporates into the air instead of soaking into the ground; or piping stormwater straight to the ocean rather than letting it refill rivers and aquifers.

We also waste water by ruining its quality. Pouring oil, paint, or excess fertilizer down drains, or allowing sewage to leak, turns a clear jug into a muddy one—still “water,” but not safely usable without expensive cleanup. Heavy irrigation in dry soils can leave salts behind, spoiling fields and aquifers. Overpumping groundwater is like spending from a savings account faster than it refills; the water will return on nature’s schedule—years to centuries—too late to help today’s users or nearby wetlands.

There’s an energy side, too. Every liter we treat, pump, and heat carries an energy bill; running long hot showers or flushing potable water is like leaving the lights on in an empty room. And when we throw away food or fast fashion, we toss the “hidden” water used to grow and make them. So wasting water isn’t about making molecules vanish—it’s about squandering freshness, location, timing, and the energy invested. Use the right quality for the task, fix leaks, water early or late, keep pollutants out of drains, and you’ll keep more books on your local shelf.

Question: does death cause the neurons in the brain to loose their properties?; does death cause any memory stored to be deleted?
Answer:
Think of the living brain as a city lit by electricity and supplied by roads bringing in fuel. Neurons are the city’s buildings and wires; their “properties” are things like their ability to keep a tiny charge across their surface and to talk to neighbors through chemical signals. When the heart stops, fuel and oxygen stop arriving. Within seconds, the electrical activity fades and you lose consciousness. Within a few minutes, the charge across neuron walls collapses, a final wave of disorganized activity may sweep through, and cells begin to swell and break. If circulation is quickly restored, some cells can recover; if not, the hardware itself—membranes, connectors, and internal machinery—starts to fail and then decay.

Memories are not files in a folder but patterns in that hardware: the strengths of connections between neurons, the little “paths” carved by experience. Death doesn’t press a delete key; it’s more like locking the library doors immediately and then, over minutes to hours, letting the shelves warp, the ink run, and the building burn. Early after the heart stops, the physical traces of memory still exist but are inactive; as damage and decomposition progress, those traces are progressively destroyed. That’s why people revived quickly after cardiac arrest often keep their memories, while after irreversible brain death and subsequent decay, the information that made up a person’s memories is lost. Cooling the brain can buy time, but without timely restoration of blood flow, both neuron function and the memories they embody are ultimately undone.

Question: why can't the water being stored at fukushima be reused for cooling?
Answer:
Short answer: you need very clean, tightly controlled water to cool damaged nuclear fuel, but the tanked water at Fukushima is “dirty” in ways that are hard or impossible to fix. Even after treatment, it still contains tritium (a radioactive form of hydrogen that is literally part of the water molecule, so filters can’t catch it) and trace leftovers of other radionuclides and salts. Pushing that kind of water back through the cooling lines would be like rinsing a wound with muddy water: it would spread contamination, raise radiation levels around equipment, increase worker dose, and accelerate corrosion and clogging of pipes and heat exchangers. For safety and reliability, operators prefer ultra‑clean, de‑salted water for injection. In fact, some water is treated and recirculated, but it has to meet strict chemistry and dose limits before it’s used.

Longer answer: reusing the stored water also doesn’t solve the “volume problem.” Picture a house with a leaky roof and a flooded basement: even if you keep mopping and reusing the same bucket of water, the leaks keep refilling the basement. At Fukushima, groundwater continues to seep in, contact contaminated areas, and add to the total volume. The reactors and buildings aren’t fully watertight, so a true closed loop isn’t possible; every liter you inject tends to leak out and mix with new inflow. Cooling now needs only a modest, steady trickle, while the tanks hold over a million tons—far more than the system can reasonably cycle through. Recirculating that much would take many years, concentrate impurities, increase gas generation from radiation splitting water, and make maintenance harder. That’s why the strategy is: minimize injection rates, treat the accumulated water to remove almost all radionuclides, accept that tritium remains, dilute it to very low levels, and discharge under monitoring—while using clean, controlled water for ongoing cooling.

Question: why did the fukushima nuclear plant switch to using fresh water after the accident?
Answer:
Right after the accident, the reactors needed cooling fast, and the easiest water on hand was the ocean. Seawater was like grabbing the nearest fire extinguisher to stop a kitchen fire: not ideal, but better than letting the house burn. Once the immediate overheating was under control, they switched to fresh water because seawater is full of salt and minerals that are terrible for a hot, delicate machine.

Picture pouring ocean water into an overheated car radiator. It cools at first, but as it boils off it leaves a crust of salt that coats surfaces like an insulating blanket, making future cooling harder. The salt also drives rust and pitting in steel, jams valves, and can damage pumps and pipes. In a nuclear plant, that means poorer heat transfer around the fuel, more wear on already stressed equipment, and far messier cleanup—tons of highly contaminated salty water that’s harder to treat. Fresh water avoids those problems: it cools better over time, limits corrosion, keeps passages clearer, and reduces the volume and complexity of contaminated waste. So the switch to fresh water was about moving from an emergency stopgap to a more sustainable way to stabilize and decommission the plant safely.

Question: when our brain begins to lose its memory, is it losing the memories themselves or the ability to recall those memories?
Answer:
Both can happen, and which one dominates depends on the cause. Think of your mind as a vast library: the memories are the books, and the ability to find them is the catalog and the librarian. With normal aging, the books are mostly still on the shelves, but the catalog is slower and the librarian takes longer to fetch what you asked for. That’s why names sit on the tip of the tongue, yet pop out later or appear instantly when you get a hint—like recognizing the right answer in a “multiple-choice” moment.

In some illnesses, though, the shelves themselves are damaged. In Alzheimer’s disease, for example, the “paper” and “bindings”—the brain cells and their connections—are gradually destroyed, so some books are partly or completely lost. When that happens, even strong cues (photos, familiar places) don’t bring the memory back, because there’s nothing left to retrieve. Head injuries or strokes can cause more sudden losses of particular “sections” of the library.

There’s also a third angle: sometimes memories are never properly “checked in” to begin with. Poor sleep, distraction, or depression can weaken the initial recording, so later retrieval feels faulty even though the memory was never well stored. In short, normal aging is mostly a retrieval slowdown, while certain diseases and injuries lead to true loss of stored memories; and everyday factors like sleep and attention affect how well new memories get on the shelf in the first place.

Question: a 5 foot section of railroad rail does not seem very flexible but a 200 foot section appears to be as flexible as a noodle with bends under a foot. how does longer length make it more flexible?
Answer:
Think of the rail’s “stiffness” as coming from its spine: the material and shape of the cross‑section set how hard it is to curve (engineers wrap this up as EI, the beam’s resistance to bending). That spine is the same whether the piece is 5 feet or 200 feet long. What changes with length is leverage and how small curvatures add up. If you push on the end, a longer piece gives you a longer lever arm, so the twisting effect (torque) inside the rail is larger for the same push. Even if the curvature at any tiny bit of the rail is small, a small bend repeated over a long distance produces a big sideways move—like a very gentle turn of a car’s steering wheel that, over miles, puts you in the next lane.

The math behind that “adds up fast.” Under an end push, the tip deflection grows roughly with the cube of the length: double the length and the tip moves about eight times more. Under its own weight, sag between supports grows even faster—about with the fourth power of length: double the span and the droop is about sixteen times greater. That’s why a 5‑foot rail feels stout while a 200‑foot rail, with the same spine, can snake around with bends under a foot: the leverage is larger, and tiny curvatures over a long run accumulate into visible, noodle‑like wiggles.

Question: is there a scientific reason why people who audition for shows like american idol but are just awful still think that they're amazing singers? are they actually hearing something different than we are when they listen to themselves sing?
Answer:
There are two big reasons. First, psychology: people are often poor judges of their own skill. If your “measuring stick” is bent, you’ll draw crooked lines and think they’re straight. Beginners use the same limited know‑how to perform and to judge the performance, so they miss their own mistakes and feel confident. Add soft feedback from friends, years of singing alone, and the fact that TV producers actively select the most overconfident bad auditions because they’re memorable, and you get the “I’m amazing!” contestant who plainly isn’t.

Second, perception: when you sing, you don’t hear what everyone else hears. Your voice reaches you through the air and through the bones of your skull, which makes it sound warmer and more powerful—like singing with a built‑in “nice reverb” filter. Your brain also predicts the sounds you’re about to make and downplays little mismatches, so small pitch errors can slip by. Some people truly have trouble sensing pitch differences or steering their voice to the right notes, so they aim correctly in their head but their “vocal steering wheel” is misaligned. That’s why a dry studio and a recording—no bone boost, no bathroom echo—can feel like a brutal mirror. So yes, they are partly hearing something different, and the rest is a mix of human bias, weak feedback, and show business selection.

Question: is a bar of soap always clean?
Answer:
Short answer: not exactly. A bar of soap can pick up germs and grime on its surface, especially right after someone uses it or if it sits in a puddle. But soap is built to solve that problem. Its molecules are like double‑sided tape: one side grabs oily dirt and microbes, the other side grabs water. When you lather and rinse, that mix gets swept away. So even if the bar isn’t “sterile,” using it with running water doesn’t spread germs; it helps remove them.

To keep a bar hygienic, give it a quick rinse before and after use, store it where it can drain and dry (think: a slotted dish, not a little bathtub), and avoid leaving it slimy. If you have cuts, very sensitive skin, or a weakened immune system—or you’re sharing with many people—consider your own bar or a liquid pump soap. In everyday use, a well-cared-for bar is a safe, effective cleaner, even if it’s not “always clean” in the laboratory sense.
