Rubbing alcohol kills many germs well, but it doesn’t “clean” very well: it lacks the soaps that lift and carry away grease, food, and dirt. On skin, the area is small and relatively clean, so alcohol works quickly. On a countertop, grime can shield microbes, and alcohol evaporates so fast that it often dries before it has stayed wet long enough to reliably disinfect. Many household sprays are designed to do both jobs at once: they contain detergents to remove soil and ingredients that keep the surface wet long enough to meet the germ‑kill time, so you get visible cleaning and more dependable disinfection in one go.

There are practical reasons too. Alcohol is flammable and produces fumes, making large-area use risky and smelly. It can also dull or damage some plastics, painted finishes, wood, or screen coatings. By contrast, surface cleaners are formulated and labeled for those materials, with clear “leave wet for X minutes” directions. None of this means alcohol can’t be used on non‑porous surfaces—it can, especially for small spots or electronics—just use 60–70% alcohol, keep the surface visibly wet for at least 30 seconds to a minute, ventilate well, and avoid materials it can harm. Most people reach for multipurpose cleaners because they clean and disinfect more reliably and safely in everyday kitchen-and-bath situations.

Question: how can we hear the voice in our head and how is it produced?
Answer:
That “voice in your head” is your brain’s way of replaying sound without using your ears. When you imagine words, the brain areas that normally process real sound—the auditory centers—become active in a softer, echo-like way. It’s like watching a private movie with the projector pointed inward: no air vibrates, no eardrum moves, but the brain reuses the same listening machinery to create the feeling of hearing. This is why inner speech can have a familiar accent, tone, or even the voice of someone you know—your brain is drawing from stored sound memories.

How is it produced? The brain gears that plan speech start to prepare what you’d say out loud, but the volume on the actual muscle commands is turned way down. Alongside that muted plan, the brain sends a prediction to the auditory system—“here’s what this should sound like.” When the auditory system receives this internal preview with no matching sound from the outside world, you experience it as an inner voice. Sometimes there are tiny, almost undetectable twitches in the throat muscles, but they aren’t required. Think of it as a built-in rehearsal stage: the scriptwriter (language areas) drafts the line, the actor (speech system) mimes it, and the audience (auditory areas) listens—all inside the same theater. This looping setup helps with planning, memory, and problem-solving, and in everyday reading it shows up as the quiet “subtitles” you hear while your eyes scan the page.

Question: why can't you remember the exact point before you fall asleep?
Answer:
Because memory needs a awake, attentive brain to “press record,” the instant you drift off isn’t saved. As you approach sleep, attention fades and the brain’s chemistry shifts; the system that normally stamps moments into memory (with the hippocampus as the main note‑taker) powers down. It’s like a librarian closing the desk while you’re still talking—those last sentences never get written on the card. By the time you actually fall asleep, you’re no longer fully conscious to witness it, so there’s nothing clear to remember.

Under the hood, the brain flips from an “encoding” mode to a “maintenance and filing” mode. Levels of alertness chemicals such as norepinephrine and acetylcholine drop, the thalamus starts gating incoming sights and sounds, and sleep rhythms (like spindles and slow waves) begin. In this state the hippocampus stops taking new snapshots and starts organizing older ones, leading to a small, normal patch of amnesia right before sleep—similar in spirit to the memory gap at the start of anesthesia. You might catch a few hypnagogic fragments if someone wakes you right then, but if not, it’s as if the camera was turned off before the final frame.

Question: if the purest white reflects all light, why isn't it a mirror?
Answer:
“Pure white” means a surface reflects all colors of visible light about equally, not that it sends the light back the way it came. A white wall is like a crowd leaving a stadium through every exit at once: light hits it and then scatters in all directions. Because the rays are scrambled, no organized picture of the world is returned to your eyes. You see brightness, but not an image.

A mirror is different not because it reflects more light, but because it reflects it in a highly organized way. Its surface is extraordinarily smooth compared with the size of light waves. That smoothness makes each incoming ray bounce off at a matching angle, like a billiard ball on a polished table. The directions stay coordinated, so the pattern of light from the scene is preserved, and you see a reflection.

Think of a lake: when the water is glassy-smooth, it’s a mirror; when it’s choppy or foamy, it turns whitish and you can’t see your face. Snow and paper are “white” for the same reason—countless tiny surfaces send light every which way. A mirror, meanwhile, could even be slightly tinted and still show a crisp image, because image-making depends on direction, not on reflecting every color perfectly.

Question: on the heels of yesterday's question, would it be possible to have a rocky planet large enough that it began nuclear fusion and turned into a star?
Answer:
Short answer: no. To turn on fusion you need two things in the core—enormous pressure and plenty of the easiest fuel to fuse, hydrogen. Even the smallest hydrogen-burning star needs about 75 times Jupiter’s mass, and brown dwarfs that briefly fuse deuterium need at least 13 Jupiters. A “rocky” planet is made mostly of heavy elements like oxygen, silicon, and iron, not hydrogen. So even if you could make it fantastically massive, it would be missing the right kind of fuel to light the fire in the first place.

What if you just keep piling on rock anyway? Picture trying to start a campfire by stacking bricks higher and higher. Gravity will squeeze the stack and heat it a bit, but past a point the material gets so stiff that squeezing it harder doesn’t make it much hotter; the electrons inside act like a packed stadium that refuses to let more people take the same seats. That “crowding” stops the temperature from ever climbing to the millions of degrees needed to fuse heavy elements. Long before you got anywhere close, a real protoplanet would also vacuum up surrounding hydrogen and helium, turning into a gas giant and, if massive enough, a brown dwarf—not a rocky star. So nature gives you two outcomes: add gas and you might get fusion in a brown dwarf or star; stick to rock and you get a bigger, denser planet, but never a self-lit sun.

Question: what are the downsides to donating a kidney?
Answer:
Donating a kidney is major surgery, so the first downsides are the short‑term ones that come with any operation. Think of it like removing a well‑built appliance from a tight cabinet: it can be done safely, but there’s prying, noise, and cleanup. You can expect pain, fatigue, and a few weeks off normal activities. There is a small risk of problems such as bleeding, infection, blood clots, or a hernia near the incision; serious complications happen in a few percent of donors, and the risk of death is very rare (about 3 in 10,000). Most people leave the hospital in 2–4 days and return to usual routines within 2–6 weeks, but recovery times vary.

Long term, you live with one “filter” instead of two. The remaining kidney usually grows a bit and works harder, giving you roughly 70–80% of your original filtering capacity. Day to day, most donors feel normal, but you lose some backup reserve—like driving with one good headlight: fine on a clear night, less forgiving in a storm. This comes with a slightly higher chance of high blood pressure, a small amount of protein in the urine, and kidney disease later in life; the absolute risk of kidney failure for carefully screened donors remains low (well under 1% over decades), but it is higher than for equally healthy non‑donors. You’ll be asked to avoid frequent use of kidney‑straining painkillers like ibuprofen, stay well hydrated, and see a clinician yearly for blood pressure, urine, and blood tests. For women, pregnancy is still usually safe, but the risk of complications like preeclampsia is higher than before donation (roughly doubling, for example from about 3–5% to 5–10%), so closer monitoring is advised.

There can also be practical and emotional downsides. Some donors face out‑of‑pocket costs or lost wages during recovery, difficulty getting new life or disability insurance, or concerns about scars or lasting numbness near the incision. A few experience regret or sadness, especially if the recipient has a poor outcome. The big picture is that donation is generally safe for well‑selected people, but it trades a small amount of physical and financial risk for the chance to help someone else. A transplant team can walk you through your personal risks and supports so you can decide with eyes wide open.

Question: how come when looking into a mirror without my glasses, stuff is still blurry far away?
Answer:
Because a flat mirror doesn’t “fix” light, it only turns it around. If you’re nearsighted, your eye focuses distant light too soon, so faraway things look blurry. Glasses work by gently bending the light before it enters your eye so it lands in focus on your retina. A plane mirror doesn’t add any bend at all—it’s like a perfect wall that just bounces the light back. So the light from a far scene stays “far-scene light,” and your eye still can’t focus it without your glasses.

A helpful picture: imagine the mirror as a window into a twin world behind the glass. Whatever is 10 miles in front of the mirror appears 10 miles “behind” it. For focusing, your eye cares about where that image seems to be, not how close the mirror’s surface is. That’s why your own face can look sharp without glasses in a bathroom mirror (your face is close, so its “twin” is close), but the distant street seen in the same mirror stays blurry. Only a curved mirror—like a magnifying makeup mirror—actually changes the light’s focus; a flat mirror never does.

Question: why can't stars fuse iron?
Answer:
Stars shine by “clicking” atomic nuclei together. When light nuclei like hydrogen or helium merge, the finished piece is more tightly glued than the two pieces were apart, and that extra tightness shows up as released energy—this is what keeps a star hot and puffy. As you build heavier and heavier elements, that payoff gets better…until you reach iron. Iron is the champion of tight binding: its nucleus is about as snugly glued as nature makes them. Try to fuse iron into something heavier and you don’t get spare energy out—you have to put extra energy in, like trying to push a boulder uphill. In other words, iron is ash, not fuel.

That difference dictates a star’s fate. In a massive star, layers keep fusing up to elements near iron, piling an iron core in the center. Because iron fusion would drain, not supply, energy, the core can no longer replenish the pressure that holds gravity at bay. The star’s center then collapses. The collapse heats things so violently that even iron gets torn back apart into lighter pieces, which soaks up still more energy, accelerating the plunge. The result is a catastrophic rebound and explosion—a supernova—while smaller stars that never reach iron simply fade into white dwarfs.

Question: if we observe a star x light years away, does that mean theres nothing inbetween here and there obstructing our view?
Answer:
Short answer: seeing a star does not mean the space between is empty. It only means that, along that narrow line of sight, nothing completely opaque is blocking the light at the wavelength you’re using. Think of a lighthouse seen through mist: you can still spot it, but the mist can dim it and make it look redder. Space is full of very thin gas and tiny dust grains; most of the time they’re more like smoke than a brick wall—partly transparent, scattering blue light more than red.

In some directions, dust clouds are thick enough to hide stars in visible light entirely, but the same stars can reappear in infrared or radio, the way night‑vision goggles pierce haze. Foreground stars almost never line up perfectly to cover a background star (they’re tiny targets on the sky), though brief alignments can cause dips in brightness (a planet transiting) or even funhouse‑mirror brightening and distortion (gravity bending light like a lens). So “obstruction” can range from mild dimming to temporary eclipses to full blackout, depending on what’s in the way and what color of light you use.

Astronomers can tell there is “stuff” in between even when the star is visible, because its light carries barcodes—narrow dark lines where intervening gas has nibbled specific colors. Even Earth’s atmosphere is an in‑between layer, blocking some ultraviolet and infrared while letting most visible light through. So if you can see the star, it means the path is transparent enough, not that it’s perfectly clear.

Question: if water has a boiling point of ~100 degrees c, why does it evaporate at room temperature?
Answer:
“Boiling point” is not a switch that turns evaporation on. It’s the temperature at which water can form vapor bubbles throughout the liquid because the push from its vapor matches the push of the surrounding air. Below that temperature, bubbles can’t grow in the middle, but the surface is a different story. Water molecules are always jiggling with different amounts of energy; even at room temperature, some have enough oomph to break free from the surface and fly into the air. That slow, steady escape is evaporation.

Picture a crowded party. Boiling is when the main doors swing open and the whole room can pour out at once. Evaporation is the trickle of energetic guests slipping out a side door one by one. Airflow and dryness make that side door wider: moving, dry air carries away escaped molecules so they don’t bump back in, which is why laundry dries faster on a breezy day. And because the quickest “guests” leave first, the remaining water loses energy and cools down—that’s the chill you feel when sweat evaporates from your skin.

why do we have different sized dogs but all the domestic cats are (roughly) the same size?
Answer:
Picture dogs as a toolbox we built on purpose and cats as a single, well‑tuned mousetrap that mostly built itself. Humans domesticated dogs much earlier and then bred them hard for many different jobs: hauling, herding, guarding, ratting, and companionship. Each job pulled body size in a different direction, and people deliberately paired the biggest with the biggest or the smallest with the smallest to exaggerate those traits. Conveniently for us, dogs have a few “growth dials” in their DNA that, when tweaked, make big changes in size, so turning those dials gave us Chihuahuas and Great Danes within a few thousand years.

Cats took a different path. They more or less invited themselves in to hunt rodents around early farms, and we mostly selected them for being tame and good at pest control, not for hauling sleds or guarding gates. Nature also keeps them near a “sweet spot” for small-prey hunting: too big and a house cat needs a lot of food and becomes clumsy for mice; too small and it loses the power and tools to be an efficient predator. On top of that, domestic cats still interbreed with wildcats in many places, which tethers their size to the wild type. So while there are bigger and smaller cat breeds (think Maine Coon versus Singapura), they hover around the same general size. In short: strong, purposeful breeding plus easy genetic knobs made dogs wildly variable; lighter selection, natural constraints, and ongoing mixing kept cats clustered around one handy, mouse‑sized design.

Question: on jupiter, will more superstorms the size the great red spot eventually form, or are the positions and types of storms relatively constant?
Answer:
Think of Jupiter as a vast, striped ocean with strong east–west currents that form the familiar bands. Those currents (jet streams) tend to stay put in latitude, so the planet keeps its stripes and certain kinds of storms prefer certain “lanes.” Within those lanes, however, storms behave like whirlpools in a fast river: they pop up, drift, merge, and fade. So the backdrop—the bands and the general storm habitats—is relatively constant, but the individual storms are not.

Superstorms the size of the Great Red Spot can, in principle, form again, but they are rare. The Great Red Spot is a gigantic, long‑lived high‑pressure whirlpool parked between two powerful jet streams that act like walls, helping it survive for centuries. We’ve seen smaller cousins appear: in the late 1990s several white ovals merged to make “Red Spot Jr.,” proof that mergers can build big, durable vortices. Juno has also revealed stable rings of cyclones around the poles, showing Jupiter can organize storms into long‑lasting patterns. Still, a Great‑Red‑Spot‑scale storm needs just the right neighborhood and a steady supply of energy, so we can’t predict when or where another will arise. In short: the lanes are steady, the kinds of storms repeat by lane, but the specific tempests—even the giants—come and go.

Question: melanin protects from the sun, but does this extra melanin in your skin come at the cost of anything else? is there any advantages to being paler?
Answer:
Think of melanin as built‑in window tint for your body. A darker tint shields the inside from harsh sunlight: it lowers sunburn risk, slows DNA damage that can lead to skin cancer, and reduces photo‑aging. The trade‑off is the same one you’d have with any shade: less light gets through to power solar‑driven jobs. In skin, one key solar job is making vitamin D using UVB light. More melanin means you need more sun to make the same vitamin D, so in places with weak or brief sunlight—high latitudes, winter, heavy clothing, indoor living—people with darker skin are at higher risk of deficiency. Historically, that deficiency showed up as rickets and bone problems in northern cities during the industrial era.

So yes, there are advantages to being paler—but they depend on where you live. Pale skin is like a lighter tint on the window: in dim environments it lets enough UVB in to keep vitamin D production going, which supports bone health and aspects of immune function. In very sunny regions, however, the same light tint can be a liability, bringing more sunburns and a higher lifetime risk of several skin cancers, and greater UV damage to skin. Evolution tuned skin color to local sunlight over many generations; there isn’t a universal “best,” only a best‑fit for the light available. In the modern world, we can bend these trade‑offs with sunscreen, clothing, shade, and vitamin D from diet or supplements.

Question: why is there a negative correlation between planet size and rotation speed?
Answer:
Short version: there isn’t a universal rule that “bigger planets spin more slowly.” In our own solar system the trend is mostly the opposite—giant planets like Jupiter and Saturn have very short days (about 10 hours), while small, close‑in rocky planets like Mercury and Venus turn very slowly. What sets a planet’s spin is not its size alone, but its history: how it formed, what it collided with, and how much it has been “braked” by tides from its star or moons.

Think of planet formation as swirling batter in a mixing bowl. Newborn planets inherit that swirl. Gas giants grew by gulping vast amounts of already‑spinning gas, which tends to leave them whirling quickly, and because they usually live far from the star, the tidal “handbrake” is weak, so they keep their fast spin. Small rocky worlds, especially those close to the star, can have their spins reworked by giant impacts and then gradually slowed by tides—like a spinning top that rubs against the table—sometimes even getting stuck in special rhythms (Mercury) or creeping to a crawl (Venus). One more source of confusion: “rotation speed” could mean how fast the surface moves at the equator or how quickly the planet completes a turn. The equatorial speed automatically grows with size, even if the spin rate is the same. If you look at some exoplanets, many big “hot Jupiters” are so close to their stars that they’re tidally locked and rotate more slowly than Jupiter does, which can create the impression of a negative correlation in that particular sample.

Question: why can bugs survive such high falls?
Answer:
Because they’re so small, air feels “thicker” to bugs than it does to us. Imagine you shrinking down to the size of a sesame seed: falling through the air would feel more like sinking through syrup than plummeting through emptiness. A bug’s body has a lot of surface area compared with its tiny weight, so air pushes up on it strongly. That drag slows the fall so much that the landing is more of a gentle plop than a crash—closer to a feather drifting down than a rock dropping.

There’s a simple size rule behind this. Weight grows with volume (three dimensions), while air resistance grows with surface area (two dimensions). As you make an animal smaller, its weight shrinks faster than the air pushing against it. The result is a very low terminal speed—the fastest speed it can reach while falling. Many bugs also splay their legs or wings as they drop, acting like built‑in parachutes. And when they land, their springy exoskeletons and bendy joints spread out the force, like excellent shock absorbers on a tiny car.

By contrast, big bodies like ours have much more weight for the amount of surface area we present to the air, so we slice through it and hit the ground hard. That’s why humans need parachutes, while ants can step off a tree and more or less shrug it off.

Question: what happens to the dust particles that get into your eyes day to day?
Answer:
Most of the dust that lands in your eyes gets handled by a built‑in cleaning crew. Think of your eyelids as windshield wipers and your tears as a thin film of soapy water. That film has three parts: a watery layer to wash, a tiny bit of oil on top to keep it from drying too fast, and a sticky layer at the bottom that grabs dust like flypaper. Each blink sweeps the trapped particles toward the inner corner of your eye, where two pin‑sized drains funnel the tear‑dust mix into your nose—one reason your nose runs when you cry. Tears also contain natural germ‑fighting chemicals that neutralize many hitchhiking microbes.

Bigger or scratchy bits trigger extra tearing to flush them out. What isn’t cleared right away can dry and collect at the corners while you sleep as that familiar “sleep” or eye gunk—a blend of dried tears, oils, skin cells, and dust. If something keeps feeling gritty, it may be stuck under the lid; rinsing with clean water or saline usually helps, and avoiding rubbing protects the clear front window of your eye from scratches. Get help if the discomfort persists, or if you notice strong pain, redness, light sensitivity, or blurry vision, which can signal a lodged foreign body or irritation that needs attention.

Question: are the stars really dead by the time we see them?
Answer:
When you look at a star, you’re seeing a snapshot from the past because light takes time to travel. The Sun’s light is about 8 minutes old, a bright nearby star’s light might be a few dozen to a few thousand years old, and a distant galaxy’s light can be millions or billions of years old. So starlight is like a postcard that took a while to arrive. But a delayed postcard doesn’t mean the sender has passed away—just that you’re seeing an earlier moment.

Whether a star is “dead by the time we see it” depends on two clocks: how long its light took to reach us and how long stars live. Most stars you can see with the naked eye are within a few thousand light-years, while stars typically live millions to billions of years. That makes the light’s travel time a tiny slice of their lifetimes, so almost all the stars you see are still shining today. A few very massive, short‑lived stars could have changed or died in that interval, but that’s rare. For truly distant objects—like faraway galaxies—we are indeed looking deep into cosmic history, where many individual stars we see in those galaxies have since evolved or died.

Question: can you prevent a sonic boom when travelling supersonic?
Answer:
Short answer: you can’t truly prevent a sonic boom if you’re flying faster than sound. Think of a speedboat outrunning its own ripples: the ripples pile up into a single V-shaped wake. In the air, those piled-up pressure waves form a thin “shell” that trails the aircraft in a cone. When that cone touches the ground, people hear the sudden jump in pressure as a boom. As long as you’re supersonic and someone lies under that invisible cone, a boom exists in principle.

What you can do is make the boom smaller and softer, and steer where it’s felt. Designers “shape” the aircraft—long, slender nose; smooth changes in cross‑section; careful engine integration—so the air is nudged gradually rather than slapped. That turns a sharp crack into something closer to a distant thump. Flying higher spreads the cone over a bigger area, reducing the peak; routing over water keeps it away from people. Think of it like putting a lampshade over a bright bulb: the light is still there, but it’s diffused and directed. NASA’s X‑59 is a famous example of aiming for a “quiet” boom rather than no boom.

Some ideas sound tempting but don’t pan out. “Noise‑cancelling for the sky” doesn’t work because a boom isn’t a simple tone—it’s a sudden, nonlinear pressure jump, so you can’t neatly erase it with an opposite wave. There are rare atmospheric setups where temperature and wind layers bend the shock upward so it never reaches the ground—like a mirage for sound. Pilots can sometimes exploit this “cutoff” to keep communities from hearing them, but it’s weather‑dependent and not guaranteed. So while silent supersonic flight isn’t possible, careful design, altitude, and routing can make it quiet enough to be acceptable.

Question: could a volcano eruption theoretically be powerful enough to launch debris into orbit?
Answer:
Short answer for Earth: no. To stay in orbit you don’t just have to go “up,” you have to go sideways so fast that as you fall, the ground curves away beneath you. Near Earth’s surface that sideways speed is about 7.8 kilometers per second—think rifle bullet times ten. The fastest volcanic jets measure at most around a kilometer per second at the vent, and most ejected rocks are far slower. Earth’s thick air then acts like molasses at hypersonic speeds, robbing what little speed remains and heating the debris. Even spectacular events like the 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption, which blasted a plume to about 58 kilometers, simply threw material on a big arc that came back down. A volcano is a powerful fire hose, not a rocket.

On smaller worlds, the story changes. Some moons have such weak gravity that “escape” takes only a few hundred meters per second. Enceladus, for example, shoots icy grains from its south‑polar geysers at roughly this speed; a fraction of those grains drift away and end up circling Saturn, feeding its faint E‑ring. Io’s towering sulfur plumes reach hundreds of kilometers high thanks to low gravity and thin air, but they still don’t achieve the several kilometers per second needed to orbit Jupiter, so most of that material falls back. So while Earthly volcanoes can’t loft debris into orbit, tiny moons can, turning their geysers into natural, slow-motion ring makers.

Question: what happens if a girl takes viagra?
Answer:
Viagra (sildenafil) is a blood‑flow booster. It relaxes tiny muscles in blood vessel walls so more blood can flow into certain tissues. In men, that helps the penis get and stay firm. In women, the same plumbing effect can increase blood flow to the clitoris and surrounding tissues, which might make them feel warmer, fuller, or more sensitive. But it doesn’t create desire or arousal by itself—the “spark” comes from the brain, emotions, and context. Studies in women have mostly shown little or no improvement in overall sexual satisfaction or libido, though select groups (for example, some women with antidepressant‑related sexual side effects) may notice modest benefits.

The side effects are similar for everyone: headache, flushing, stuffy nose, dizziness, upset stomach, and sometimes a blue‑tinted vision or light sensitivity. It can lower blood pressure, so mixing it with nitrates (often used for chest pain) or certain heart and blood‑pressure medicines can be dangerous. It’s not approved for treating sexual problems in women, and it’s generally not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding unless a doctor prescribes it for another medical reason. In short, Viagra can increase “water pressure in the pipes,” but it doesn’t turn on the sprinkler system. If sexual pain, low desire, or arousal issues are a concern, a clinician can help pinpoint causes and suggest safer, more effective options.

Question: why does the infinite series 1/n diverge?
Answer:
The harmonic series adds 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … and asks whether these ever settle down to a fixed total. A simple way to see they don’t is to group the terms in blocks whose sizes double: take (1), then (1/2), then (1/3 + 1/4), then (1/5 + 1/6 + 1/7 + 1/8), and so on. In the third block each term is at least 1/4, so that block sums to more than 1/2. In the fourth block each term is at least 1/8, and there are four of them, so again the block sums to at least 1/2. Every new block contributes at least another half. Because there are infinitely many blocks, the total grows past any number you name; it never settles. That is what it means to diverge.

A picture to keep in mind is stacking floors in a tower: each new floor is thinner than the last, but you add more rooms each time. Even though the rooms keep getting thinner, each floor still raises the building by at least half a unit. With infinitely many floors, the height goes up without bound. This also shows a common pitfall: it isn’t enough that the individual terms shrink to zero; they must shrink fast enough. For 1/n they shrink too slowly, so the pile keeps creeping upward forever.

Question: have all visible (to the naked eye) stars been named / cataloged?
Answer:
Short answer: cataloged, yes; named, mostly no. Under a really dark, moonless sky, a person with good eyesight can see on the order of a few thousand stars at once, and roughly five to six thousand over the whole year as the sky changes. Only a few hundred of these have traditional names like Sirius or Betelgeuse, which the International Astronomical Union has standardized. The rest are identified by systematic labels—think “Greek letter + constellation” (like Alpha Centauri) or a catalog number—so they have reliable “addresses,” even if they lack nicknames.

As for catalogs, astronomers have been thorough. Classic lists such as the Bright Star Catalogue include essentially every star bright enough for typical naked-eye viewing, and modern surveys like Hipparcos and Gaia have measured positions and motions for all of them (and over a billion fainter ones). In other words, every star you can normally see has a precise entry somewhere—many have several. The main exceptions are brief guest appearances: a new nova that suddenly flares into visibility might be “new” for a while, but once spotted it too gets an entry. If the sky were a town, all its residents are in the phone book, but only some go by memorable nicknames.

Question: what temperature would be required to ignite the earth's atmosphere, and would it be possible for humans to ignite our atmosphere?
what is the bottom of a tectonic plate like?
Answer:
Imagine a tectonic plate as a thick, stiff pancake riding on a very slow, warm taffy. The “bottom” of the plate isn’t a clean, shiny underside like a frying pan; it’s a blurred transition where hard, cool rock gradually gives way to hotter, softer rock that can creep over millions of years. There’s no open space down there—just rock pressed against rock under immense pressure. At those depths it’s hot enough that some minerals weaken and tiny amounts of melt or trapped fluids can form, making the base a little more slippery, like a glacier sliding on a thin film of water. The result is a fuzzy boundary rather than a sharp line: solid on both sides, but the lower side behaves more like putty than brick.

This “underside” also varies from place to place. Under oceans the plate is relatively thin and warm, so its bottom meets the soft layer sooner; under old continents the plate is thicker, with deep, keel-like roots that reach farther down before they soften. Near mid-ocean ridges, fresh hot rock rises and the base is especially warm; in subduction zones, the descending plate’s underside gets altered by fluids and heat as it dives. Up close (if you could go there), you’d see rough, fractured rock, not a smooth hull—more like the underside of sea ice, with bumps and channels—yet the whole thing still moves because the softer rock below can slowly flow, and thin films of melt and fluids at the base help it along.

Question: why do you "see stars" when you rub your eyelids?
Answer:
Those “stars” are called phosphenes—visual sensations created without light. Your eye’s light-sensing layer, the retina, is like a camera sensor wired to your brain. It normally fires when light hits it, but it doesn’t actually care why the wiring is active. When you rub your eyelids, you gently squash and tug the retina. That mechanical nudge makes its cells send electrical signals, and your brain, seeing activity on the “vision line,” interprets it as light. Think of a doorbell that rings whether you press the button or wiggle the wires—either way, the chime sounds.

The patterns you see—sparkles, arcs, or swirling grids—come from how the retina is laid out and how pressure waves ripple across it. Different parts of the retina map to different parts of your visual field, so a ring of pressure can look like a ring of light. Similar “fireworks” can happen when you stand up too fast, cough hard, or have a migraine aura; brief changes in blood flow or nerve activity can make visual cells misfire, and the brain again “draws” light from those signals.

A little gentle rubbing is usually harmless, but don’t press hard or often. Strong or habitual rubbing can irritate the cornea, raise eye pressure (a concern in glaucoma), and in rare cases contribute to retinal problems. If you notice sudden flashes without touching your eyes, especially with new floaters or a curtain-like shadow, see an eye doctor promptly.

Question: i heard somewhere that if one could see the andromeda galaxy in its entirety, it would look 2-3 times the size of the moon, is this true?
Answer:
Short answer: if you count the whole galaxy, Andromeda is much bigger than that. Its full disk spans about 3 degrees on the sky, while the full Moon is about 0.5 degrees. So Andromeda is roughly six Moon-widths across. The “2–3 times the Moon” figure underestimates its true angular size.

The confusion comes from brightness. Andromeda is like a giant, faint chalk drawing spread across the sky, while the Moon is a small, bright sticker. Your eyes easily catch the Moon’s glare, but they struggle with Andromeda’s very low surface brightness. Under dark skies you usually see only the bright central “smudge,” which is about one to two Moon-widths across. With binoculars you can trace more of its length, and with long-exposure photos—where a camera patiently gathers light—you reveal the full, six-Moon-wide sweep.

Question: stars collapse once they start producing iron at their core. how much iron would i need to throw into the sun to kill it?
Answer:
Iron doesn’t “poison” a star the way sugar might ruin a car engine. In very massive stars, an iron core builds up because fusion keeps stacking heavier “ash” in the center. Iron is special only because fusing it doesn’t release energy—so once the core is mostly iron and heavy enough, the star runs out of pressure support and the core collapses. The Sun is too small to ever reach that stage on its own; a few spoonfuls, mountains, or even a planet’s worth of iron tossed in would be like throwing paperclips into a blast furnace: they melt, sink, and barely affect the fire.

To “kill” the Sun by iron-core collapse, you’d have to assemble an iron core in its center nearly as heavy as a whole star—about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass in iron alone. That’s more iron than the Sun’s entire mass. Even dumping Jupiter (or a thousand Jupiters) of iron wouldn’t come close. And if you somehow could add that much material, you wouldn’t neatly switch the Sun off; you’d be turning it into a different, far more massive and violently unstable object long before an iron core quietly formed. In short, there is no realistic amount of iron you can throw into the Sun to “kill” it—the Sun will end its life on its own schedule, swelling into a red giant and then settling as a white dwarf, with no iron-triggered collapse along the way.

Question: can a venomous snake commit suicide by biting itself ?
Answer:
Short answer: usually no. Venomous snakes are largely protected from their own venom. Think of venom molecules as keys that fit specific locks in a victim’s body. Snakes have evolved “locks” that their own keys don’t easily open, and they also carry proteins in their blood that act like bouncers, grabbing and neutralizing much of their venom if it strays inward. So if a snake accidentally bites itself, it’s unlikely to die. That said, some venoms—especially those of vipers—are very harsh on tissue, so a self-bite can still cause a painful local wound where the fangs went in.

It isn’t absolute protection. Biology is messy, not magic. A huge dose, a direct hit into a large vein, severe illness, or species with weaker self-resistance could, in theory, cause serious trouble, and bites from a different species can be dangerous. But confirmed deaths from true self-envenomation are exceedingly rare. Also, “suicide” implies intent; snakes that bite themselves are usually confused—overheated, stressed, or mistaking their own body for prey that smells like food—rather than trying to end their lives.

Question: is it "healthier" to remove your wisdom teeth even if they are not bothering you?
Answer:
Short answer: not automatically. Think of wisdom teeth as the back-row seats in a crowded theater. If they’ve come in straight, fully above the gum, and you can brush and floss them like any other tooth, they often can stay without harming your health. But if they’re tilted, trapped partly under the gum, or buried in the jaw, they can become crumb-collectors that invite decay and gum infection—sometimes quietly, before you feel pain.

Keeping them carries risks mainly when they’re hard to clean or pressing on the tooth in front: cavities, gum disease, occasional cysts (rare). Removing them is a small operation with its own risks: pain, swelling, infection, “dry socket,” and, rarely, temporary or permanent numbness of the lip or tongue, or sinus issues for upper teeth. Evidence is mixed: some guidelines advise against routine removal of symptom-free, disease-free wisdom teeth, while others favor earlier removal to avoid problems later. Despite the common belief, wisdom teeth don’t reliably “push” the front teeth crooked.

A sensible approach is watchful care guided by your dentist or oral surgeon. They’ll look at position, how cleanable the area is, and X‑rays that show space, root shape, and any early damage to the neighbor tooth. If the tooth is quiet, healthy, and easy to monitor, leaving it in and checking it periodically is reasonable. Removal makes more sense if you’ve had repeated gum swelling, decay, damage to the next tooth, pockets that trap food, you can’t keep the area clean, or you’ll need certain orthodontic or jaw surgeries. Age matters too: surgery is usually easier in the late teens and early 20s, but that alone isn’t a reason to remove healthy, problem-free teeth.

Question: why are there no "natural" artificial sweeteners?
Answer:
Because “natural artificial sweetener” is a contradiction in terms. “Natural” refers to substances that occur in nature and can be extracted from plants or other living things. “Artificial sweetener” usually means a sweet-tasting molecule that does not occur in nature and is invented or heavily modified by people (like sucralose or saccharin). Think of two light switches: one switch says “Where does it come from?” (natural vs. human-made), the other says “How many calories does it add?” (caloric vs. low/zero-calorie). People often flip the second switch in their minds and call anything zero-calorie “artificial,” but that mixes up two different ideas.

There are, in fact, natural sweeteners that are very low- or zero-calorie. Stevia comes from a leaf (steviol glycosides), monk fruit from a fruit (mogrosides), and some sweet-tasting proteins occur in plants (thaumatin, brazzein). Even sugar alcohols like erythritol and xylitol exist in small amounts in fruits and plants, though we usually make them at scale by fermentation or processing, which can blur the “natural” label on packages. So the short answer is: you can have natural, low-calorie sweeteners—but you can’t have something that is both “natural” and “artificial” at once. The confusion comes from using “artificial” as a stand-in for “zero-calorie,” when it really means “not found in nature.”

Question: is there a gradient at which bicycles become less efficient than walking?
how come when ice is in my cup, and i rotate the cup, it stays in the same position?
Answer:
What you’re seeing is inertia at work. When you quickly twist the cup in your hand, you’re only directly turning the cup itself. The water inside doesn’t grab on tightly—it’s slippery—so it doesn’t instantly spin with the cup. Only the thin layer of water touching the cup wall gets tugged, and it slowly drags the rest along. The ice is like a passenger on a bus without a seatbelt: when the bus turns suddenly, the passenger wants to keep going straight. If you keep rotating the cup steadily for a while, the water will eventually start to rotate as a whole, and then the ice will “join the ride” and turn with it. If the cup were filled with something thicker, like honey, the ice would get dragged along much sooner.

If by rotate you mean tilting the cup, the effect is a bit different but just as simple: the water surface always tries to stay flat like a calm pond under gravity, and the ice floats on that flat surface. So when you tip the cup, the water re-levels relative to the ground, and the ice rides that new “mini-lake,” seeming to ignore the cup’s tilt. In short, quick twists make the ice lag because of inertia and weak dragging by the water; tilts make it look steady because water keeps a level surface and the ice floats on it.

Question: why do chickens lay unfertilized eggs?
Answer:
Because a hen’s body runs on a built‑in schedule. Think of her reproductive system like a bakery with a conveyor belt: every day or so it sends out a “yolk” onto the line. As it travels, the body adds the egg white and then the shell, whether or not a rooster has shown up. If sperm happens to meet the yolk right at the start, the egg is fertilized; if not, you still get a perfectly normal egg—just one that will never develop into a chick.

This daily rhythm is guided mainly by daylight and hormones. Long, bright days tell the “bakery” to keep baking, and it takes about 24–26 hours to assemble one egg from yolk to finished shell. The system doesn’t stop to ask, “Do we have an order?”—it just keeps the line moving. That’s why hens lay even when no rooster is around.

In the wild ancestors of chickens, this conveyor belt ran more slowly and seasonally: they laid a small batch (a clutch) and then stopped to sit on them. Humans, however, bred domestic chickens to be champion layers and often use long lighting periods and remove eggs from the nest, which keeps the hormones saying “make another.” The result is many more unfertilized eggs than would occur in nature.

Question: if fevers are the immune system's response to viral/bacterial infection, why do with try to reduce them? is there a benefit to letting a fever run its course vs medicinal treatment?
Answer:
Think of fever as your body turning up the thermostat to make the house uncomfortable for unwelcome guests. A modest rise in temperature can slow down some germs and helps certain immune cells work faster. But heat has a price: your heart beats quicker, you lose more fluid, you feel lousy, and in people who are very young, older, pregnant, or have heart and lung problems, that extra strain can be risky. So while fever is a tool, it’s a blunt one—useful, but not harmless.

We lower fevers mainly to help you feel better, sleep, and drink fluids—comfort isn’t trivial; good rest and hydration aid recovery. Medicines like acetaminophen or ibuprofen don’t “turn off” your immune system; they just ease the heat and aches. For most routine infections, treating fever for comfort doesn’t meaningfully change how long you’re sick. If a mild fever is tolerable, it’s reasonable to let it be; if you’re miserable or the temperature is high (around 102–103°F or 39–39.5°C), it’s reasonable to treat. Seek medical care sooner for babies under 3 months with any fever, for fevers above about 104–105°F (40–40.5°C), for fever lasting more than 3 days, or if there are red flags like confusion, stiff neck, trouble breathing, severe dehydration, or a widespread rash. This is general advice; your own risks and comfort should guide whether you let a fever run or cool it down.

Question: does staring at a computer for 4-5 hours a day harm you in any way?
Answer:
Short answer: for most adults, 4–5 hours of computer use a day doesn’t cause permanent eye damage. Screens at normal brightness don’t “burn” the retina. But they can leave you uncomfortable. Focusing on one distance for a long time is like keeping a camera’s autofocus motor humming nonstop—your eye muscles get tired, leading to eye strain and headaches. We also blink less at screens, so the eye’s “windshield wipers” don’t spread tears well, causing dryness, burning, or blurry moments. Long sitting and peering forward can irritate your neck, shoulders, and back. If you use screens late at night, the bright light can nudge your body clock later and make it harder to fall asleep.

A few habits prevent most of this. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds to relax your focus. Blink on purpose; lubricating eye drops can help if you’re dry. Keep the screen about an arm’s length away, with the top at or slightly below eye level; increase text size and contrast so you’re not squinting. Reduce glare and harsh overhead light, and avoid air blowing into your eyes. Stand up and stretch your back, neck, and wrists every hour. In the evening, dim the screen, use a warmer “night” mode, and try to unplug 1–2 hours before bed. Regular eye checks and the right glasses reduce strain; if symptoms persist or vision changes, see an eye care professional.

Question: does a jar of flies weigh less if the flies are flying around in the air rather than if they're at the bottom of the jar?
Answer:
If the jar is sealed and sitting on a scale, the weight is the same whether the flies are resting or flying. When they’re standing, their feet push down on the glass. When they’re flying, their wings push air downward; that air then presses on the bottom and sides of the jar, which pushes on the scale. Either way, the jar-plus-contents passes the same total push to the scale once things settle. You might see brief wiggles when they take off or land, but on average the reading is unchanged. Think of a helicopter in a closed room: even if it hovers, the room’s floor still carries the load via the downdraft.

If the jar is open, some of that downward-blown air can spill out into the room instead of pressing on the jar. In that case, part of the flies’ weight is supported by the surrounding air and furniture, not by the jar, so the scale can read a little less while they hover. Put a lid on, and the “bill” comes back to the jar. In short: sealed jar, no weight change; open jar, slight dip while flying. Flies don’t get to cheat gravity—they just hand the tab to either the jar or the room.

Question: why can't dental plaque be dissolved with a solvent, why must we scrape it off?
Answer:
Think of dental plaque as a living, sticky film—like a slimy wallpaper—made by bacteria. These bacteria build a fortress around themselves using a glue-like mix of sugars, proteins, and bits of DNA called a biofilm matrix. Water and mild rinses can’t dissolve this glue, just as water won’t lift dried caramel off a plate. The “solvent” strong enough to melt this matrix would also be harsh enough to burn your gums or damage your enamel. So the safe, effective way to remove it is to physically break that matrix with brushing and flossing—the toothbrush is your scraper, applying shear force to peel the wallpaper off the wall.

If plaque sits undisturbed, minerals from your saliva seep in and harden it into tartar (calculus). Now it’s not just sticky wallpaper—it’s more like barnacles on a boat hull, made of calcium phosphate crystals similar to what teeth themselves are made of. Dissolving those barnacles would require acids or chelators strong enough to chew through the same minerals your teeth are built from, so chemical “melting” would damage the hull along with the barnacles. That’s why dentists use metal scalers or ultrasonic tools: they chip off the rock without eroding the tooth.

In short, plaque resists safe solvents because it’s a resilient biofilm, and tartar resists them because it’s literally mineralized stone. Daily brushing and flossing sweep away the fresh slime before it hardens; professional scraping removes the barnacles once they’ve set.

Question: in movies, characters who are shot and losing blood are often urged to stay awake. does trying to maintain consciousness really improve the chances of survival in such a situation?
Answer:
Short answer: urging someone to “stay with me” doesn’t stop the bleeding, but it can help in ways that matter. When someone is losing blood, the brain is getting less oxygen. The body may make them drowsy or knock them out to save energy—like a city dimming the lights during a water shortage. Talking to them won’t fix the “leak,” but if they’re awake they keep their throat muscles working so the airway stays open, they can follow instructions, and you can judge their mental state from moment to moment. The stress of staying engaged may also squeeze blood vessels a bit and help maintain pressure for a short time, but that effect is small and temporary.

What truly improves survival is fast, simple first aid: stop the leak and call help. Press hard directly on the wound with whatever clean cloth you have; if a limb is bleeding heavily and won’t stop, use a tourniquet if you know how. Lay them flat, keep them warm, and keep them still. Don’t give food or drink. If they become unresponsive but are breathing, roll them onto their side so the tongue and any vomit don’t block breathing; if they’re not breathing, start CPR if trained. Keep talking to them if they’re awake—it’s reassuring and useful—but remember the lifesavers are pressure, positioning, warmth, and rapid transport, not sheer force of will.

Question: why isn't copper as reactive as pottasium or any other of the alkaline metals?
Answer:
For metals, “reactive” mostly means “how eager is the atom to give away its outer electron.” Picture the nucleus as a hand holding a set of house keys (the electrons). In potassium, the last key is on a long, floppy string far from the hand, so it’s easy to snatch—very little energy is needed to remove it. In copper, the keys are pulled in closer and gripped more firmly. Copper’s extra protons pull harder, and the electrons in its inner, crowded “d” layer don’t block that pull very well, so the outer electron feels a strong tug. As a result, copper has a higher ionization energy (it costs more energy to pry off an electron), so it doesn’t hand over electrons as readily as potassium.

There are two helpful consequences of this tighter grip. First, potassium gladly becomes K+ and releases a lot of energy doing so, which is why it reacts violently with water. Copper, by contrast, doesn’t react with water because giving up electrons isn’t energetically favorable in that setting; in fact, copper more often prefers to stay as metal or only slowly forms a thin oxide layer that protects the rest of the metal beneath. Second, copper’s electron arrangement is relatively stable (its “d” shell is filled when it forms Cu+), which further reduces its urge to react. In short: potassium throws its outer electron like a hot potato; copper keeps its electrons on a tight keyring.

Question: why does the word "mama" so often mean mother in different languages, even in languages that aren't closely related?
Answer:
Because babies are the ones who “name” their parents first, languages often follow what babies can say most easily. The earliest clear syllables infants produce are built from simple lip sounds like m, p, and b, paired with the open “ah” vowel: ma, pa, ba. Imagine a baby with lips together making a humming “mmm” while feeding, then popping the mouth open into “ma.” Double that easy syllable—because repetition is simple and catchy—and you get “mama.” Caregivers everywhere are delighted, hear “ma,” and treat it as a call for mother. Through thousands of tiny moments of praise and repetition, the baby sound becomes the family word, and in many communities it eventually hardens into the everyday term for “mother.”

This is why “mama,” “papa,” “dada,” and similar pairs show up in lots of unrelated languages: not because the languages are related, but because the same small human mouths and the same parental feedback create the same solution. It’s a case of convergence, like different cultures independently inventing the ladder because everyone has to climb. It isn’t universal—some languages use other words for “mother,” and a few even flip the mapping (in Georgian, for example, “mama” means father). The broad pattern, though, comes from a mix of biology (what sounds are easiest first) and behavior (adults eagerly assigning those sounds to the people who matter most).

Question: what do tiny spiders eat?
Answer:
Tiny spiders eat even tinier creatures. Think of them as miniature lion cubs hunting the crumbs of the bug world. Freshly hatched spiderlings and very small species go after springtails, mites, aphids, booklice, thrips, and baby flies like fruit flies and fungus gnats. Web-makers catch whatever small fliers their silk can snare—gnats and midges are common—while tiny hunters that don’t use webs pounce on ground-dwelling specks that hop or shuffle over leaves and soil.

They choose prey they can overpower, then turn it into a drink rather than a meal to chew. A quick nip delivers venom and digestive juices, and the spider sips the liquefied insides—call it “bug broth.” When animal prey is scarce, some tiny spiders will supplement with pollen, nectar, or sugary droplets called honeydew, and a few will scavenge very soft dead insects. On rare occasions they’ll even take other tiny spiders. Picture them as pocket-sized pest controllers, quietly harvesting the smallest moving dots in the landscape.

Question: what do tiny spiders eat?
Answer:
Tiny spiders eat even tinier bugs—think snack-sized prey for a snack-sized hunter. Their menu includes gnats, midges, fruit flies, aphids, springtails (tiny flea-like soil jumpers), mites, and booklice in houses. Web-builders catch these in hair-thin nets that act like invisible sticky hammocks in the air, while little jumping or ground-dwelling spiders chase them down like miniature cats pouncing on mice.

Newly hatched spiders often start by living off a bit of stored yolk, then move on to very small, soft-bodied prey or even scavenge dead insects. Some will sip sweet liquids such as nectar, pollen, or honeydew when they find it—like grabbing a juice box between meals—but meat is still their main food. Different tiny spiders use different tactics: some wait patiently in their webs, others stalk and leap, but almost all are busy clearing the world of bugs you can barely see.

Question: what causes mosquitos to be super attracted to some people, and completely ignore others?
Answer:
Think of a mosquito as a tiny flying nose with a heat sensor and a needle. From far away it homes in on the exhaust plume of carbon dioxide you breathe out. As it gets closer, it switches to vision, favoring dark, high‑contrast shapes, and then to short‑range cues: the warmth of your skin and the scent cocktail on its surface. People who exhale more CO2 (bigger bodies, faster metabolism, pregnancy), run hotter, move more, or wear dark clothing are easier for that “flying nose” to find. Fresh sweat itself doesn’t smell much, but once skin bacteria start breaking it down, they release lactic acid and other volatiles that many mosquito species love. A single beer can also nudge attractiveness upward for a couple of hours, likely by changing breath and skin chemistry.

Up close, your skin is its own little perfume factory, and the recipe is largely set by your skin microbes and your genes. Some people’s microbes churn out compounds that act like neon “open” signs to mosquitoes; others produce more neutral or even masking scents. That’s why two people sitting side by side can be very different targets. Blood type can play a small role in some species (type O tends to be a bit tastier than type A), but it’s minor compared with overall odor chemistry. Also, “ignored” can be an illusion: some people are bitten but don’t swell or itch much, so the bites go unnoticed.

If you want to be less interesting to them, change the signals they use. Use a proven repellent on exposed skin (DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus), wear light‑colored clothing that covers ankles and wrists, and sit near a fan to blow away your CO2 plume and body scents. Think of it as scrambling the mosquito’s radar so it flies past you in search of a clearer signal.

Question: what is the purpose of a prostate, and why does it cause problems for older men?
Answer:
The prostate is a small, walnut-sized gland that sits just below the bladder and hugs the urethra—the tube that carries urine out of the body. Think of it as a ring-shaped “pump station” on the pipeline between the bladder (water tank) and the penis (hose). Its main job is to make a special fluid that mixes with sperm to form semen. This fluid nourishes and protects sperm and helps them move, and the muscle in the prostate squeezes during ejaculation to push semen out while also helping keep urine and semen in their proper lanes.

It causes trouble in older men mostly because it tends to keep growing throughout adulthood under the influence of male hormones, especially a potent form of testosterone. As the “donut” grows, it tightens around the “straw,” narrowing the urethra and making urination harder—leading to a weak stream, frequent trips at night, urgency, or a feeling of not emptying completely. This is a common, non-cancerous enlargement. Age also brings more low-grade inflammation and stiffer tissue, which add to the squeeze. Separately, the risk of prostate cancer rises with age; it usually starts in the outer part of the gland and may cause no early urinary symptoms, which is why screening discussions are important. Not every man develops problems, but when the ring around the straw swells, the plumbing shows it.

Question: does the sun experience "tides" due to influence of it's satellites (the planets)?
Answer:
Yes. Just as the Moon raises ocean tides on Earth by pulling a little harder on the near side than the far side, the planets raise tiny “tides” on the Sun. Because the Sun is a hot, fluid ball of gas, it can be very slightly stretched along the line to a planet. The biggest contributors are Jupiter, then Venus and Earth. But the effect is minuscule: the expected surface distortions are only millimeters to, at most, a few centimeters—on a star 1.4 million kilometers across. Picture a pot of soup boiling with meter-high bubbles; now imagine trying to spot a ripple the thickness of a coin riding on top of that. The Sun’s own churning motions are so large that they completely swamp these planetary tugs.

It helps to separate this from another effect people often mention: the Sun also “wobbles” around the solar system’s common center of mass because of the planets’ gravity, especially Jupiter and Saturn. That wobble moves the whole Sun as a unit; it doesn’t stretch it, so it’s not a tide. Some have wondered whether the planets’ gentle tugs might pace the Sun’s 11‑year activity cycle, but most evidence says the tides are far too weak to do that. In short, the Sun does have tides caused by its planets, but they are real in principle and vanishingly small in practice.

Question: when the mars rover went to mars were they able to remove all bacteria and small life from it? if not could any of the bacteria be able to live in the harsh conditions of mars? and how do they obtain soil samples looking for bacteria if it could possibly be from the rover itself?
Answer:
Short answer: no spacecraft is perfectly sterile. Before launch, Mars rovers are assembled in hospital‑like clean rooms, wiped with disinfectants, and many parts are literally baked in giant ovens to kill hardy microbes. That said, you can’t cook the whole rover without ruining electronics, and some spores can hide in tiny crevices. The Viking landers of the 1970s came closest to “as sterile as we can make it,” but even they weren’t microbe‑free.

Could stowaway microbes live on Mars? The Martian surface is like Antarctica crossed with the Atacama Desert, placed under a tanning bed: extreme cold, almost no liquid water, intense ultraviolet sunlight, and oxidizing salts in the soil. Most Earth microbes would be fried, dried, or chemically burned. A few tough spores might survive dormant for a while, especially if shaded under dust or inside the rover, but actually growing and spreading needs liquid water and milder conditions that the open Martian surface doesn’t provide. Missions also steer clear of places where transient liquid water might exist, to avoid even that small risk.

To make sure samples aren’t “rover confetti,” engineers control and track contamination from start to finish. Drills, scoops, and sample tubes are ultraclean and heat‑sterilized; tubes are sealed immediately after coring. The rover carries “witness” tubes—empty tubes that ride along and capture anything the rover sheds—so later, scientists can subtract that fingerprint from the real samples. Instruments also run blanks and calibration checks to spot any rover‑derived chemicals. When samples come to Earth (for missions that cache them), they’ll be opened in specialized labs with their own controls, letting scientists tell Martian signals from any earthly hitchhikers with high confidence.

Question: how can a speaker produce more than one sound at a time?
Answer:
Think of sound as ripples in air. A loudspeaker makes those ripples by moving its cone in and out. If you want two sounds at once—say two musical notes—you don’t need two cones. You simply add the two wiggles (electrical signals) together and feed the sum to the speaker. The cone then follows that combined wiggle, creating a single, complicated ripple pattern in the air. Your ears act like a little frequency-sorting machine, teasing the blend back apart so you hear both notes. It’s just like dropping two pebbles into a pond: the ripples overlap and travel through each other, yet you can still see both patterns at once.

There are limits. A cone is happiest when its motion is “linear,” meaning it can follow the summed wiggle faithfully. Push it too hard and it starts to add extra, unwanted ripples (distortion), making new tones that weren’t in the original mix. To keep things clean, many speakers split the job: big woofers handle low ripples, small tweeters handle fast, fine ripples, but each still produces many frequencies in its range at once. In fact, even a single “note” from a violin is really a bundle of frequencies, and a speaker reproduces all of them together—one surface dancing a complex choreography that our ears untangle back into separate sounds.

Question: why is electricity blue?
Answer:
Electricity itself has no color—just like wind has no color. What you see as “blue electricity” is the surrounding air lighting up. When a spark or lightning bolt rips through air, it shoves electrons around so hard that they crash into molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. Those molecules get briefly energized and then calm back down by giving off light. The “favorite” colors that nitrogen and oxygen emit are mostly blues and violets, so the glow of a spark or lightning often looks blue-purple to our eyes.

Change the environment and the color can change. In a neon sign, the gas is neon, so the glow is orange-red. Sodium makes a bright yellow, copper can look green, and very hot arcs can appear white because they’re so intense they produce a mix of many colors at once. In thin, wispy “corona” around power lines on damp nights, the same air glow shows up as a faint bluish haze. And in a perfect vacuum, with nothing to excite, electricity would be invisible—no air, no glow.

Question: what actually happens when your empty stomach "growls"?
Answer:
That “growl” is simply your gut’s plumbing at work. The muscles of your stomach and small intestine squeeze in waves to push along whatever is inside—mostly air and a little fluid when you haven’t eaten. When those waves mix and move pockets of gas, they make echoes, like squeezing a half-full water bottle and hearing the slosh and gurgle. Food usually muffles the sound, so an emptier stomach acts like a drum, making the rumble easier to hear.

Why does it happen most when you’re hungry? Between meals, your gut runs a housekeeping cycle—think of a janitor doing a nightly sweep or a washing machine’s rinse cycle. Guided by signals from your brain and hormones, these stronger, periodic waves clear out leftovers and nudge bacteria and crumbs downstream. This “cleaning” tends to roll through every 90 to 120 minutes when you’re fasting, which is why the timing can feel rhythmic. It’s normal, it can also occur after eating, and it gets louder if you’ve swallowed more air (talking while eating, fizzy drinks) or if gas is being made. The takeaway: a growling stomach isn’t scolding you; it’s just housekeeping you can hear.

Question: do shampoo function as a body wash as well as a product labeled body wash will?
Answer:
Short answer: yes, shampoo will clean your body, but it’s not optimized for it. Think of it like using dish soap to wash your car—it removes dirt, but it may strip away the protective wax. Shampoos are built to lift oil and product from hair and scalp and often include ingredients that coat hair to make it feel smooth. On skin, that can translate to either extra dryness (from stronger cleansers) or a light film that some people find waxy or pore‑clogging. Body washes, by contrast, are tuned for skin: they usually use gentler cleansers and add more skin-friendly moisturizers like glycerin to help prevent tightness and flaking.

In practical terms, using shampoo as a body wash in a pinch is fine, especially if your skin is not sensitive. For everyday use, a product labeled “body wash” is more likely to keep skin comfortable. If you must double-duty, pick a gentle or “sulfate‑free” shampoo with minimal fragrance, avoid dandruff shampoos (they contain medicated ingredients meant for the scalp), and rinse well to avoid residue. If your skin feels tight, itchy, or you notice breakouts on the body, switch back to a true body wash and consider following with a light moisturizer.

Question: elon musk talks about using water and carbon dioxide on mars to refuel rockets using a process called "sabateir" why don't we do this on earth instead of using fossil fuels?
Answer:
On Mars there are no oil fields, so you have to “cook your own fuel.” The Sabatier process is the recipe: take carbon dioxide from the Martian air and hydrogen from water, add energy, and you get methane (rocket fuel) and water; split water to get oxygen for burning. It’s perfect there because CO2 is abundant, water ice exists, and every kilogram of fuel you don’t have to launch from Earth saves a fortune. On Earth, we can do the same trick—and we already do in small “power-to-gas” plants—but there’s a key difference: Sabatier is not an energy source, it’s just a way to repackage energy. To make methane you first need lots of electricity to split water into hydrogen, then you combine that hydrogen with captured CO2. When you finally burn the methane, you just get the CO2 back. It can be close to carbon‑neutral only if the electricity is clean and the CO2 you use is pulled from the air or from a biogenic source.

Think of it like converting cash to gift cards and back again: every exchange takes a cut. Turning electricity into hydrogen, then into methane, and later back into motion or electricity throws away a big slice of the original energy, while using that electricity directly—say, in an electric car or heat pump—keeps much more. Add the costs of capturing CO2, building electrolyzers and reactors, and the risk of methane leaks (a potent greenhouse gas), and the fossil alternative still wins on price in many places. That’s why Sabatier fuels aren’t replacing everything, but they do have a niche: storing excess wind and solar from summer to winter, feeding existing gas pipelines and boilers, and supplying fuels for planes, ships, and high‑temperature industry where wires can’t easily do the job. In short, on Mars it’s a lifeline; on Earth it’s a specialized tool we’ll likely use where direct electrification falls short.

Question: when beryllium-8 undergoes alpha decay, is there a difference between the alpha particle emitted and the helium atom left behind?
Answer:
Short answer: no. In nuclear terms, both products are the same thing—a helium‑4 nucleus. An “alpha particle” is just a helium‑4 nucleus without electrons. When beryllium‑8 breaks up, it doesn’t leave a quiet helium atom sitting at the original spot while another helium nucleus flies away. Instead, it “snaps” into two identical helium‑4 nuclei that shoot off in opposite directions, like two identical balls released from a compressed spring.

What about the electrons? A neutral beryllium atom starts with four of them, but the breakup is so sudden and the two nuclei move off so briskly that the electrons can’t keep up; they’re left behind or stripped away. Immediately after the decay you therefore have two bare alpha particles and some free electrons. Later, if the nuclei pass through matter, each can capture two electrons and become an ordinary neutral helium atom. So the only difference you might see is not in what they are at the nucleus level, but in whether and when they pick up electrons—eventually both can become helium atoms, but at the moment of decay they are just two identical alpha particles.

Question: do insects have a sleep schedule?
Answer:
Yes—most insects keep a kind of sleep schedule, though it doesn’t look like our single long night. Insects enter a sleep-like state: they become still, adopt a typical resting posture, respond less to gentle disturbances, and if kept awake, they “catch up” later. This rest is timed by an internal 24‑hour clock, like a tiny wristwatch set by sunrise and sunset. Even in constant darkness, many insects keep a near‑daily rhythm, showing that the clock is built in and only fine‑tuned by light, temperature, and food.

What that schedule looks like depends on the species and its lifestyle. Day‑active insects such as honeybees largely sleep at night—you can picture a bee dozing on a flower as the light fades—while many mosquitoes and moths flip the script and sleep by day. Fruit flies sleep mostly at night but also take a midday “siesta.” Social insects break rest into many short naps: worker ants grab hundreds of power‑naps that add up to several hours, while queens sleep longer. These schedules are flexible, too. A young “nurse” bee working inside a dark hive may adopt round‑the‑clock shifts with fragmented sleep, then switch to a tidy night‑resting pattern when she becomes a forager. In short, insects don’t follow a human‑style bedtime, but they do keep time—and they sleep on a plan.

Question: why was poor eyesight not genetically removed when humans/prehumans were in their nomadic phase of evolution?
Answer:
Evolution is not a perfect eye doctor; it’s more like a gardener who trims only what clearly harms the plant before it sets seed. Many kinds of “poor eyesight” either show up late (like age-related near-vision loss), are mild, or can be worked around in a cooperative group. In small forager bands, someone with weaker distance vision could still gather plants, make tools, care for children, or follow others on a hunt. Good near vision can even be an asset for fine work. Because people with less-than-perfect vision could still survive and have children, the penalty on reproduction—the only thing evolution “counts”—was often small. On top of that, traditional outdoor life tends to delay or reduce myopia, so the problem was likely rarer and milder than it is in today’s indoor, book-and-screen-heavy world.

Genetically, eyesight isn’t a single on/off switch; it’s more like a mixing board with hundreds of tiny sliders. That makes “removal” by natural selection slow and messy. Many variants have very small effects, some help in other ways (trade-offs), and new mutations keep reappearing—like weeds drifting in on the wind. There’s also evidence that some gene patterns tied to myopia track with traits favored in certain environments, such as long schooling. Put together: the cost before reproduction was limited, the trait is highly complex and shaped by environment, cooperation softened the edges, and fresh genetic variation keeps arriving. The result is what we see today—eyes that are good enough for most of our evolutionary history, but increasingly out of tune with modern habits.

Question: prosthetics: can someone born without a limb (rather than losing it after birth) use advanced prosthetics controlled by nerves and neural pathways?
Answer:
Yes—with some caveats. Advanced prosthetics need a control signal, like a microphone needs a voice. That signal can come from tiny electrical pulses in muscles, from the nerves that used to go to the missing limb, or, in research settings, directly from the brain. People born without a limb often still have the main “wires” (the big nerves) and some nearby muscles, even if the hand or foot never formed. Surgeons can reroute those nerves into healthy muscles in the upper arm or chest (a procedure called targeted muscle reinnervation), essentially plugging old wires into new speakers so the prosthetic has a clear signal to listen to. Sensors on or in those muscles then let the user open and close a hand, move a wrist, or switch grips. Many children and adults with congenital limb difference already use “myoelectric” prostheses that read muscle signals from the residual limb; when the limb is very short or the signals are weak, nerve rerouting or implanted sensors can strengthen the control.

The brain is surprisingly ready for this, even without prior experience using that limb. Think of a conductor whose orchestra lost its violin section at birth—the score for the violins is still in the folder. With practice and feedback, the conductor can direct new instruments to play those parts. Studies show the brain keeps a hand “map” that can be recruited for controlling a prosthetic, and users can learn to produce distinct, reliable signals with training. Restoring a sense of touch is harder: if sensory nerves are present, gentle electrical stimulation can sometimes create pressure or tap-like sensations; if not, vibration or skin stretch elsewhere on the body can stand in as “subtitles” for touch. Outcomes depend on how much nerve and muscle is available, the level of the limb difference, surgical options, and training time—but in principle, and increasingly in practice, people born without a limb can control advanced prosthetics using their own nerves and neural pathways.

Question: do women live longer than men naturally or is the disparity caused by a predisposition of men to do more dangerous activities?
Answer:
Both. Across almost every country and time period, women live longer than men, and the gap comes from two stacked layers: a built‑in biological edge plus a large behavioral layer. The biological layer shows up even before “dangerous activities” enter the picture: baby boys die more often than baby girls, men fared worse than women during COVID-19 at the same ages, and female biology seems to protect the heart and immune system for longer. Having two X chromosomes acts like carrying a spare parts kit—if one copy has a glitch, the other can compensate—while testosterone tends to push metabolism and risk-taking biology harder, more like driving a fast car with thinner brake pads.

The behavioral layer then widens or narrows the gap depending on culture and era. Men, on average, smoke more, drink more heavily, work in riskier jobs, drive and fight more, and visit doctors later. When those habits change, the gap moves: in places and periods where men smoked far more than women, men died earlier; as women’s smoking rose, the difference shrank; in regions with heavy male alcohol use, the gap ballooned. Even when lifestyles are similar, a small difference usually remains, suggesting a biological “floor” to the disparity, but much of the excess can be traced to modifiable behaviors.

So the short answer: women do have a natural longevity advantage, and men’s tendency toward risk—both biological and social—magnifies it. Taming the changeable part (tobacco, alcohol, speed, violence, skipped checkups) can narrow the gap, but probably won’t erase it entirely.

Question: why does egg turn white when you cook it?
Answer:
An egg white starts out clear because it’s mostly water with proteins folded up into tiny, tidy bundles that let light pass through. Heat makes those proteins unfold—like coiled springs straightening out—and exposes sticky spots along their length. The now-sticky strands grab one another and knit into a loose net that traps water. In cooking terms, the fluid turns into a soft gel.

It turns white because that new protein net is full of countless tiny pockets and strands that scatter light in all directions, the same way clouds and milk look white. Instead of light slipping straight through, it bounces around and comes back at you, so you see white. Gentle heat forms a looser, tender net; high heat tightens it, squeezing out water and making the egg firm and rubbery.
